events.title: Exhibit | Centering Philippine and Filipinx American Histories: Selections from The Bancroft Library
events.description: The Bancroft Library's collections of materials relating to the Philippines span nearly 500 years. Highlights in this exhibit include a transcript of an Inquisitorial trial from 1646, a prayer book written in the Cebuano language, and UC Berkeley Filipino student publications from 1905 to the present. The exhibit also features selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author Jessica Hagedorn, including typewritten drafts of her novels, poetry, song lyrics, and a screenplay, as well as childhood drawings and writings.Bancroft's renowned Latin American collections offer up intriguing examples of documents produced by the Spanish Empire as it exploited the islands' natural, cultural, and human resources. Examples include the transcript of the Inquisitorial trial of two women accused of being spiritual mediums, a manuscript written in the Jawi script, which is based on Arabic script promising religious freedom to the Muslim residents of the island of Mindanao, and materials regarding the trade between Manila and Mexico.The personal papers and published works of UC Berkeley professors Bernard Moses (1846-1931) and David Barrows (1873-1954) document their early involvement with American colonialism in the Philippines, especially their work in redesigning the Filipino education system. In the aftermath of a brutal war, Americans viewed education as a tool for pacifying a conquered population. Documentation of these professors' white supremacist views is contrasted with the work of Filipinx and Asian American scholars who use their words to critique colonialism and its racist underpinnings.Educational opportunities have brought students from the Philippines, and later Filipinx American students, to Berkeley since the early 20th century. The exhibit includes examples of four student publications — two published in the first two decades of the 1900s and two more contemporary examples — that provide evidence of these students' political engagement and their determination to make their voices heard.Selections from the personal papers of acclaimed author and performance artist Jessica Hagedorn are also on display, including examples of her novels, plays, poetry, song lyrics, a screenplay, childhood drawings, and writings. Hagedorn employs a kaleidoscope of pop culture references, songs, images, and quotes from historical figures, and a galaxy of characters representing various cultures, classes, genders, races, and nationalities in her depictions of the Philippines and Filipinx America.Open hours may vary. Please view the The Bancroft Library hours (https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/bancroft) page for the most up-to-date information.

events.title: Exhibit | De y para el pueblo / By and for the People: Revolutionary Mexican Prints
events.description: The exhibit features highlights from The Bancroft Library's extensive collection of prints. The show examines how a Mexico City-based artists collective, the Taller de Gráfica Popular (Workshop for Popular Graphic Art), built an artistic legacy, tracing its roots from José Guadalupe Posada's portrayals of everyday Mexican life, to its enduring influence on artists on both sides of the U.S.-Mexico border today.

events.title: Exhibit | Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley
events.location: The Rowell Exhibition Cases, Doe Library, 2nd floor
events.description: In 1985, UC Berkeley students, with support from faculty, staff, and labor unions, transformed the campus into the heart of a powerful anti-apartheid divestment campaign. They organized rallies, teach-ins, and shantytown encampments to protest the university's financial ties to companies profiting from South Africa's system of racial segregation. Divestment Now! Student Activism and the Anti-Apartheid Movement at UC Berkeley highlights a movement that mobilized thousands, politicized a new generation, and laid the groundwork for ongoing struggles for racial and economic justice.

events.title: Exhibit | Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.location: Bernice Layne Brown Gallery (inside Doe Library)
events.description: In August 2023, thirty international artists, writers, scientists, and filmmakers traveled 450 nautical miles across the Marshall Islands with youth and elders from the nation's Indigenous communities. That expedition, Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here (https://www.ourlifeishere.org), was not one to witness ruin, but a return: an act of honoring ancestral lands, the struggles of those who came before, and the enduring presence of Marshallese life today. An exhibition in Doe Library's Bernice Layne Brown Gallery gathers reproductions of works made during and after the voyage together with rare books, maps, and photographs drawn from UC Berkeley's own libraries—The Bancroft Library, the Earth Sciences & Map Library, the Environmental Design Library, Morrison Library, and the Main (Gardner) Stacks. Six cases move from the conditions that shaped the voyage, through the journey itself, to the living Marshallese knowledge and youth-led activism that carry it forward. Interpretive text is punctuated by QR codes linking to films, poems, and the organizations at the center of the project. This presentation is part of a series of exhibitions, installations, courses, and public programs across UC Berkeley during the 2026–27 academic year (https://cici.berkeley.edu/komij-mour-ijin-our-life-here-uc-berkeley), guided by the Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative. The exhibition was co-curated by independent curators Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll, in partnership with UC Berkeley librarians Becky Miller and Susan Powell. The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell.

events.title: Photography Installation: Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands
events.description: At Giannini Hall, 36 photographs selected from the recently published Remembering the Future: Nuclear Testing, Rising Seas, and The Marshall Islands (Radius Books, © 2026) by Mark Klett and William L. Fox extend the two men's decades-long collaboration tracing the nuclear history of the American West and the broader Pacific sphere. Installed along the building's main hallway, the images move between the physical remains of nuclear testing—bunkers, craters, camera towers reclaimed by jungle—and the everyday textures of Marshallese life: canoe building, weaving, seawalls raised by hand. Paired with archival images from the testing era and drawn from Fox's field notes and essays, the photo essay holds both histories at once: the violence of nuclear history, and the resilience of a culture that continues to inhabit these islands. An artist and curator-led tour with Mark Klett and William L. Fox will take place on September 23 at 4 PM. —Mark Klett is a photographer interested in the intersection of places, history and time. His background includes working as a geologist before turning to photography. Klett has received fellowships from the Guggenheim Foundation, the Pollock-Krasner Foundation, the National Endowment for the Arts, and the Japan/US Friendship Commission. His work has been exhibited and published widely in the United States and internationally, and is held in over eighty museum collections worldwide. He is the author/co-author of twenty books. Klett is Regents' Professor Emeritus at Arizona State University where he taught for forty years. —Presented by the UC Berkeley Environmental Arts and Humanities Initiative in partnership with the Rausser College of Natural Resources.The Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here expedition was organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, and supported by Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell. Special thanks to independent curators of UC Berkeley Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here exhibitions Amy Kisch and Svea Lin Soll. Kõmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley is made possible with support from the Stellar Blue Fund, Cape Farewell, and the Kramlich Art Foundation. —Image Credit: "The concrete bunker destroyed by the 15-megaton Bravo explosion"2023. Mounted archival digital print, 36 x 48 inches each. Titles and dates as published in Remembering the Future. Courtesy of the artist.

events.title: Video Exhibition: Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here
events.description: Worth Ryder Art Gallery and the VIDRINE present four artists' video responses to nuclear history, colonialism, and climate change in the Pacific, made in the wake of the Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here voyage. In Anointed, poet and Marshall Islands Climate Envoy Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner stands on Runit Dome at Enewetak Atoll, the concrete cap the United States built over radioactive debris from its nuclear tests, and speaks to radioactive racism and the long quest for peace and justice. The video was directed by Dan Lin and produced by Pacific Resources for Education and Learning. Michael Light's BRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023 returns to the site of the Castle Bravo nuclear test, tracing its mark on the landscape across nearly seventy years. In Mammoth, Michael Pinsky carries a mammoth tooth from England's eroding Norfolk coast to the Castle Bravo crater at Bikini Atoll, linking the mammoth's climate-driven extinction to today's rising seas. David Buckland's videos of his Bikini Texts projected into and on the waves inside the Bikini Atoll. The words projected, including 'Our Life is Here,' all reflect on the Marshallese culture, the traumatic nuclear explosions detonated on Bikini and the rising sea levels.Featured Artworks: Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner — AnointedMichael Light — BRAVO, ECHO 1954–2023Michael Pinsky — MammothDavid Buckland �� Bikini TextsAbout Kōmij Mour Ijin / Our Life Is Here at UC Berkeley (http://ourlifeishere.org)In 2023, thirty international artists, writers, scientists, and filmmakers traveled 450 nautical miles across the Marshall Islands with Marshallese youth and elders. This expedition—organized by Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, Michael Light, and David Buckland, with support from Stellar Blue Fund and Cape Farewell—was not one to witness ruin, but a return: an act of honoring ancestral lands, the struggles of those who came before, and the enduring presence of Marshallese life today. Throughout 2026–27, the project runs across campus in exhibitions at Doe Library, Giannini Hall, Memorial Glade, Worth Ryder, and BAMPFA, along with courses and public programs. It culminates in an exhibition of original works at the David Brower Center, September 2027 – February 2028. ourlifeishere.org (https://art.berkeley.edu/ourlifeishere.org)About Worth Ryder Art Gallery / VIDRINE (https://art.berkeley.edu/gallery)The Worth Ryder Art Gallery (WRAG) is an educational art space that has served as a cultural and artistic resource and community center for undergraduate and graduate students, faculty, alumni, and the Bay Area community since 1960, and is a central social and artistic hub of the UC Berkeley Department of Art Practice. The gallery supports students in exhibiting their artwork in a professional gallery context, serves as an exhibition platform for emerging contemporary artistic strategies, and brings challenging and thought-provoking artwork to the UC Berkeley campus. It is named after painter and founding chair of the department, Worth Ryder. VIDRINE is Worth Ryder Art Gallery's ancillary space showcasing video, digital art, and installation. It is located around the corner from the Worth Ryder Art Gallery in the lobby of the Anthropology and Art Building.

events.title: Transportation Planning Fundamentals for California Streets
events.description: Description In today's environment, local streets and roads need to be planned, designed, built or retrofitted, operated, and maintained to provide safe, comfortable, and environmentally sustainable travel for all users of all ages and differing levels of mobility. Ideally these local streets and roads should provide for all modes, including walking, bicycling, taking transit, and driving. Local streets and roads must be operationally functional to allow for emergency response, road maintenance, and overall truck movement of goods. This course covers the planning and conceptual design of sustainable, multimodal, local streets and roads; the history of multimodal surface transportation planning in the US; the policy environment for sustainable, multimodal transportation; how to integrate multimodal transportation into the local urban planning process; and how to design local streets, intersections, crossings, and interchanges consistent with the sustainable, multimodal approach. The course's discussion of the legislative environment is focused on California. The course spans the full range of key areas from characteristics of the local roadway system, analysis of flow and capacity, traffic/transportation operations, traffic control devices, pedestrian/bicycle facilities, and surface transit operations to traffic safety and advanced analytical methods. The course is taught by a team of professional engineers and planners who practice in the private and public sectors with a collective experience exceeding 100 years. Key learning concepts to be highlighted throughout the three days of intensive training include: managing conflict between/among surface modes, striving for a balanced approach to promoting multiple modes along the same right-of-way (ROW) or crossing each other, promoting safety between modes and for each mode on local streets and roads, options for separating or prioritizing modes in layered networks, planning for multimodal travel at the local level wherever possible, managing multimodal transportation operations efficiently, promoting economic development and livability (in addition to access and mobility), and the best practices in multimodal surface transportation infrastructure planning and sustainable land development for livability. Topics IncludeThe Multimodal Transportation Planning Process and Legal Framework Data Collection, Quantitative Analysis, and Travel Forecasts Environmental Analysis and CEQA New Trends (SB 743) Evaluation and Prioritization of Multimodal Transportation Projects Public Participation & Involvement, Dealing with Controversy Freeway Multimodal Considerations The New Transit/Multimodal Role for Arterials and Collectors Multimodal Traffic Signals Pedestrians and ADA Accommodations: It's the Law Pedestrian Safety and Economic Development Residential Streets: Livability and Quality of Life Multimodal Auditing Techniques and Walking Tour On-Street Bicycling and Ensuring Bicycle Safety Bicycle Paths: Putting it All Together Surface Mass Transit Planning Concepts Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) & Light Rail Transit (LRT) Design Elements and Issues What You Will Learn Attendees will gain an understanding and appreciation of the necessary balance of all surface modes in building, operating and maintaining a functional and multi-modal infrastructure. Multi-modal streets that make effective and efficient use of rights-of-way represent an essential framework for developing and maintaining vital urban and suburban centers and neighborhoods. Trainees will learn the planning role of multimodal surface transportation in the U.S. today, and the processes that are used to achieve planning objectives, including how data is collected and used in multimodal transportation analyses. Attendees will gain an understanding of how regional plans and forecasts affect local land use and transportation plans. They will also learn how environmental analyses and public participation fit within the multimodal transportation planning process, including key impacts on existing networks, legal requirements, and how to resolve conflicts of multimodal transportation projects. In addition, attendees will:Learn the basic principles for highway operations in California, the latest innovations of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) in freeway multimodal functions, and how to relate regional travel pricing policies to successful multimodal operations (e.g., Bay Area) Learn about parallel relationships of multimodal measures on arterial and collector streets for proper freeway operation and multimodal interactions, as they meet over critical junctions such as signalized intersections Learn a full range of treatments for pedestrian and bicycle movement in urban and suburban communities alongside a successful movement of vehicles, including bus priority considerations and success stories throughout the state and nation, with a focus on available tools and design techniques in harmony with the complete streets concepts Learn about the effects of parking considerations as well as innovative pricing programs (e.g., SF Park) and how they influence modal choice and healthy economic development Learn the key design and operational strategies to improve the safety and mobility of bicyclists in a multimodal environment and gain an understanding of which bikeway design options are appropriate for land use contexts in the state Learn how the various transit modes are essential components of well-planned communities from big cities, such as Los Angeles and San Francisco, to suburban municipalities to small towns Learn key planning, design, and operational elements pertaining to LRT and BRT in a multimodal operational environment (e.g., Gold Line LRT, Van Ness BRT) Learn how to better integrate public transit modes with each other, with other modes of surface transportation, and with land use; and the role of the state's metropolitan regions and local governments in this integration Who Should Attend This course is intended for local (i.e., cities and counties) urban planners, transportation planners, and planning technicians, as well as transportation and land use consultants. Both new and experienced planners will benefit from this course. The course is primarily appropriate for urban and suburban perspectives, but may be relevant to rural areas that are subject to urban growth challenges.

events.title: Exhibit | An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: An Archive of Archives: Roman Vishniac's Exhibition History | New York, 1971-72 shares some of Vishniac's iconic images documenting Jewish life in Central and Eastern Europe between 1930 and 1940. The Magnes acquired the Roman Vishniac Archive (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/collections/museum/jewish-art/vishniac/) in 2018, thanks to an unprecedented gift by the late Mara Vishniac Kohn (1926-2018). The collection is comprised of thousands of original prints, negatives, and archival materials documenting the long international career of Roman Vishniac (1897-1990), a Russian-born modernist photographer most notable for documenting Eastern-European Jewish life in the years immediately preceding the Holocaust. Vishniac's work has been celebrated in exhibitions and publications since the 1940s. The gift represents one of the most important acquisitions made by The Magnes since its founding in 1962, and one of inestimable value to UC Berkeley for insight and research into 20th-century East European Jewry, and beyond. As this important collection is being painstakingly processed and documented, the Magnes is beginning to share new findings with the public. An archive of this magnitude is bound to reveal many discoveries, opening up new perspectives on the life and work of a globally recognized photographer, and allowing us to revisit some of the salient moments in his career. A veritable "archive of archives," the collection also contains among its treasures substantial documentation of some of Vishniac's early exhibitions. With this installation, the Magnes is sharing with the public a group of images from an exhibition originally presented at the Jewish Museum in New York (October 19, 1971, until January 23, 1972). The show later traveled to universities, libraries, art galleries, and Jewish museums in New York State, New Jersey, Washington, DC, Illinois, and California. It showcased a selection from a broader project, titled The Concerns of Roman Vishniac: Man, Nature, and Science. The original project, now lost in its entirety, had been created under the direction of Cornell Capa (1918-2008) as part of a series entitled The Concerned Photographer, under the auspices of the International Fund for Concerned Photography. The exhibition included microscopic photography, and a multimedia installation about the photographer's scientific images, along with many of Vishniac's most iconic images from Eastern Europe, which are presented here. The exhibition closes Dec 17, 2026. Major support for the Magnes comes from the Helzel Family Foundation, the Magnes Museum Foundation, the Magnes Leadership Circle, and the the Office of the Chancellor at the University of California, Berkeley. The Magnes is committed to providing exhibitions and programs that are accessible, welcoming, and inclusive of our community.If you have any questions about accessibility or require accommodations, please contact us at magnes@berkeley.edu (mailto:magnes@berkeley.edu) or 510.643.2526.

events.title: Exhibit | Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon | Part 1
events.organizer: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art & Life
events.description: Nancy Lee Katz: A Private Pantheon (https://magnes.berkeley.edu/exhibitions/nancy-lee-katz-a-private-pantheon/) explores the artist's decades-long effort to photograph artists, writers, musicians, and thinkers she admired, including Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, Stephen Sondheim, Maya Lin, Roy Lichtenstein, and Seiji Ozawa. Created in the intimate environments of personal studios and workplaces, these 133 portraits look behind public accolades to reveal a quiet, private presence. Unfolding in two parts (fall and spring), the exhibition presents, for the first time, the entirety of Katz's Pantheon. Part 1 | Sep 2 - Dec 17, 2026 Part 2 | Jan 19 - May 13, 2027Nancy Lee Katz (1947–2018) was a prolific photographer who spent her life documenting people and places. Katz was born to a Jewish family in Los Angeles and traveled extensively in her youth, exploring Europe and Morocco before beginning work as an assistant film editor and still photographer. From 1986 to 2010, she created a remarkable pantheon of portraits, focusing on artists, musicians, writers, and thinkers whose work she respected, though she never sold nor published her prints. She also pursued music, art, and travel, documenting traditional cultures worldwide. Katz's independence and passion left a lasting mark on those who knew her. Sachs, who has made this exhibition possible through his generous gift of Nancy Lee Katz's Pantheon (2024.1), loan of additional prints, and gracious consultations. events.title: Exhibit | Time Capsules: Exploring the Permanent Collection

events.description: In celebrating 15 years at UC Berkeley, Time Capsules revisits ten out of the over thirty exhibitions presented since the Magnes opened the doors of its new academic home to the public. events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar (Postdoc)
events.description: Cris Woroch, Arnold O. Beckman Postdoctoral Fellow, UC BerkeleyPolymer design with new monomers & post-polymerization modificationsPolymeric materials are essential for modern life, but current production and disposal methods pose significant environmental harm. Most commodity polymers are constructed from a small set of petrochemical precursors that are non-renewable, are carbon-intensive to produce, yield materials that are challenging to recycle, and offer limited chemical diversity. My work focuses on designing new materials from renewable feedstocks and new methods to upcycle the materials used today. I will present recent work on the construction of new materials from lignocellulose-based furfural and carbon dioxide and the selective oxidation of polyethylene surfaces. In each, I will highlight how careful control of polymer microstructure yields new properties not met by commodity materials.Biography: Cristián (Cris) Woroch is originally from Oakland, California. He earned his undergraduate degree in chemistry at Pomona College, where he worked as a Beckman Scholar with Prof. Nicholas Ball to develop SuFEx methods for medicinal chemistry. In 2019, he moved to Stanford University for his graduate studies with Prof. Matthew Kanan. In his Ph.D. work, he developed new methods of synthesizing performance-advantaged polymers from lignocellulose and carbon dioxide as an NSF Graduate Research Fellow and Center for Molecular Analysis and Design (CMAD) Fellow. During his graduate studies, he also worked at the National Laboratory of the Rockies in the BOTTLE Consortium under Dr. Gregg Beckham as a DOE Science Graduate Research Fellow and at X, the Moonshot Factory (formerly known as Google X) as a Ph.D. Resident in plastics recycling on Project Materra. Currently, he is an Arnold O. Beckman Postdoctoral Fellow at UC Berkeley with Prof. John Hartwig, where he studies catalytic post-polymerization modification approaches for polymer upcycling.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.title: Finding Your Northern Star: Designing Work That Aligns with Who You Are (2026 Fall NOW Encore Series)
events.description: 2026 NOW Encore Series (https://hr.berkeley.edu/development/career-development/workshops) Many professionals reach a point where their role no longer feels fully aligned with who they are, what they value, or how they want to contribute. This sense of being "stuck" can lead to disengagement, uncertainty, or the feeling that one's potential is underutilized — even in meaningful work. This interactive workshop offers participants space to pause, reflect, and reconnect with a clearer sense of direction. Using the concept of a personal Northern Star, participants will explore how their talents, aspirations, and the causes they care about can be integrated into a guiding framework for career decisions. Rather than assuming that fulfillment requires an immediate job change, the session expands the conversation to include multiple pathways for alignment: reshaping aspects of a current role, integrating meaningful work through projects or hobbies, or intentionally preparing for a future transition. Through a guided Northern Star exercise and a priority-mapping activity, participants will identify what matters most to them at this stage of their career, recognize areas of alignment and misalignment, and clarify where they want to invest their time and energy. The emphasis is on practical reflection that leads to actionable insight.Learning Outcomes: –Articulate the key elements of your personal Northern Star that bring clarity to your professional direction. –Assess alignment across different areas of your work and life to identify realistic opportunities for change without requiring an immediate job move. –Apply a simple prioritization approach to determine next steps that support both personal fulfillment and professional sustainability.Registrants will be sent a Zoom link and bCal invite as the virtual workshop date draws near.

events.title: Cognition Colloquium: Compressed Representations for Memory, Reinforcement Learning, and Curiosity
events.description: Memory systems operate under finite resources and capacity, retaining some information while forgetting the rest. A central problem is how to organize experiences into representations that balance efficiency and fidelity according to task demands. This is challenging because very similar experiences sometimes require different responses or lead to different outcomes. For example, two nearly identical mushrooms may be edible or poisonous. Sparse coding separates similar experiences by expanding neural representations, but taken to an extreme, it implies a separate representation for every choice and stimulus. I propose that lossy compression offers an alternative: by discarding redundant information while preserving task-relevant differences, compression supports both memory discrimination and reinforcement learning. I will present theoretical, computational, behavioral, and neural evidence for this account in a memory discrimination task, implicating compressed encoding and retrieval in the higher-order visual cortex and the hippocampus. I will then extend this principle to naturalistic reinforcement learning, where participants in a Super Mario environment learned latent reward structure through eat-or-leave decisions across thousands of unique mushrooms. As participants explored, their policies and state representations became increasingly compressed. Moving from extrinsic to intrinsic rewards, I will examine how compression shapes curiosity-driven information seeking as participants freely browse Wikipedia. Finally, I will discuss how brain networks may implement compression. Compression offers a unifying account of how neural systems extract relevant structure from experience to support memory, learning, and decision-making.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "The Value of Codifying Organizational Knowledge"
events.description: Abstract:Codification allows knowledge to be replicated and transmitted independently of those who acquired it. Historically, it has required human articulation, leaving much organizational knowledge tacit and new firms relearning through experience much of what older firms already know. Artificial intelligence (AI) relaxes the articulation constraint by codifying knowledge directly from operational records. We formalize AI as a codification technology in models of firm dynamics. We define the value of codifying organizational knowledge as the aggregate output gain if entrants were "born old," drawing knowledge from the distribution of mature firms. We show that this value is measured by two statistics—the relative size and lifespan of mature firms—and attained in the limit of perfect codification. U.S. data suggests potential gains of up to one GDP, even if AI automated neither production nor innovation. Across industries, gains vary widely and are largely orthogonal to existing measures of AI exposure.

events.title: North Korea's Messianic Cause
events.organizer: Berkeley Center for the Study of Religion
events.description: What if North Korea was understood less as a nuclear-armed nation state and more as a religious society, one built around worship of the Kim family? It's not as far-fetched as you think. Pyongyang is already the center of one of human history's greatest personality cults: One populated by thousands of statues, busts, mosaics, obelisks, museums and monuments dedicated to state founder Kim Il Sung and his son and grandson, Kim Jong Il and Kim Jong Un. But before Pyongyang was known as the capital of the Kim dynasty, it was better known as the "Jerusalem of the East," the most thoroughly Christianized city in all of Asia. Among the earliest and most fervent converts to the brand of American Presbyterianism that arrived in the city in the late nineteenth century were the very parents and grandparents of Kim Il Sung. Kim grew up in a devout home, attending church every Sunday, teaching Sunday school, performing in church plays and learning to play the organ. The doctrine and ritual he imbibed as a young boy helped him shape the core of the state that he would rule, beginning at age 33 in 1945, until his death a half century later.Jonathan Cheng is the China bureau chief for The Wall Street Journal, overseeing coverage of the world's second-largest economy across politics, economics, business, technology, and society. Jonathan leads a team of two dozen correspondents and researchers in Beijing, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Taipei, Singapore, and New York, with responsibility for the Chinese mainland and Taiwan. Previously, Jonathan was the Korea bureau chief for The Journal, running coverage of North Korea and South Korean politics and business. He began his career as an intern in The Journal's Hong Kong bureau and also worked as a markets reporter in The Journal's New York office. Jonathan speaks English, Cantonese and Mandarin Chinese, French, and Korean. A native of Toronto, Jonathan graduated from Princeton University with a degree in history. He lives in Beijing and has traveled to North Korea twice.

events.title: Seminar 218, Psychology and Economics (joint with Public): Dmitry Taubinsky - "Policy Design with Frame-Dependent Preferences: A Robust and Practical Approach to Normative Pluralism"
events.description: Abstract: People's choices often depend on the frame in which they are made. For example, marketing can influence how consumers value goods, the immediacy of a choice can influence consideration of intertemporal tradeoffs, and public policy can shape people's preferences. In many cases, such framing effects are not "mistakes"—they reflect equally legitimate but mutually inconsistent normative values. We develop a welfare criterion that admits this normative pluralism yet still provides precise money-metric estimates of policies' welfare effects. The criterion amounts to minimizing (across policies) the maximum money-metric deadweight loss (across frames). It is the unique criterion satisfying a set of natural axioms. We study the criterion's general properties and illustrate its application to a variety of policy design questions, including "sin taxes," provision of commitment opportunities, active-choice versus optimal default regimes, nudges, and the regulation of marketing and advertising.

events.title: Commutative Algebra and Algebraic Geometry Seminar: A nearly coordinate-free counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture
events.description: Speaker: Ruslans Aleksejevs, UC BerkeleyOn July 19, 2026 (the day Spain beat Argentina 1–0 in the World Cup final), Levent Alpöge posted a counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture. Four days later, on July 23, Rémy van Dobben de Bruyn published 'A nearly coordinate-free counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture', a blog post explaining the geometry behind the example. We'll begin this talk with a little background: what the conjecture says, where it came from, and how it's connected to the Dixmier conjecture. Then we'll follow van Dobben de Bruyn's exposition through the geometric construction, working with an equivalent formulation of the Jacobian conjecture in algebraic geometry. We'll introduce the geometric background along the way, with the focus on getting a clear picture of the construction.

events.title: David Chandler Lecture in Physical Chemistry
events.description: Nancy Makri, Professor, University of IllinoisReal-Time Path Integral Methodology for Quantum Dynamics in Condensed-Phase EnvironmentsSince the mid-1990s the iterative, tensor-based quasi-adiabatic propagator path integral (QuAPI) methodology has enabled numerically exact, fully quantum mechanical simulations of system-bath dynamics. Recent work showed that one can further disentangle the path integral variables through the rigorous small matrix decomposition (SMatPI), which leads to iterative propagation with matrices of minimal size equal to that of the system's reduced density matrix (RDM). By eliminating tensor storage, the SMatPI algorithm enables the simulation of multistate systems and long-memory processes. Combination with modular path integral (MPI) decompositions suitable to systems with a locally one-dimensional topology enables iteration in space and time, leading to linear scaling with system size and propagation length. The methodology has been extended to anharmonic environments, whose effects on the RDM can be equivalent to those from an effective harmonic bath or give rise to novel features arising from essential, non-removable anharmonicity. Recent work has shown that the quantum paths entering the path integral expression can be mapped on graphs, whose properties can be exploited to arrive at novel algorithms that allow the efficient treatment of static disorder and the simulation of processes that involve thousands of system states (regardless of the nature of the system Hamiltonian).

events.title: Seminar 237 - Macroeconomics/Monetary Economics: "Strategic Complementarity and Persistence in Linear-Quadratic Mean Field Games"
events.description: Abstract: We study the relation between strategic complementarities and aggregate persistence in linear-quadratic mean field games with interactions in states and actions. The framework provides local approximations to common macroeconomic problems, including capital accumulation and multiproduct pricing. We show that the equilibrium aggregate dynamics coincide with those of a single-agent linear-quadratic control problem in which state and action curvatures are adjusted for strategic interactions. This result gives conditions for equilibrium existence, establishes uniqueness, and links strategic interactions to aggregate adjustment. We establish conditions under which stronger state complementarities increase persistence, while stronger action complementarities reduce it, even in multidimensional problems whose underlying matrices are not simultaneously diagonalizable. Under these conditions, internalizing state complementarities makes the utilitarian planner's allocation more persistent, while internalizing action complementarities makes it less persistent. Aggregate-only payoff terms can reinforce or offset these effects. With common shocks, we give conditions under which individual and aggregate dynamics can be combined to identify strategic interactions and model parameters. Finally, we extend the analysis to interactions through higher moments of the state distribution.

events.title: A Journalist's Path to Leadership on Global Justice and Climate
events.description: Nicholas Kristof grew up on an Oregon farm and became a Pulitzer Prize winning columnist for the New York Times, best-selling author and maker of TV documentaries. He has chronicled war, genocide and climate injustice, and has been held at gunpoint in more countries than he cares to remember. Kristof recovers from his travels by raising apples and grapes on his family farm and confronting climate change directly. Nicholas Kristof is a columnist at The New York Times and a two-time winner of the Pulitzer Prize. He grew up on a farm in Oregon, graduated from Harvard, earned a First in law at Oxford University as a Rhodes Scholar, and then studied Arabic in Cairo. He was a foreign correspondent for The New York Times in Hong Kong, Beijing and Tokyo, and then served as editor of The Sunday New York Times. After 9/11, he became an op-ed columnist. Aside from his Pulitzers, for coverage of China's Tiananmen democracy movement and for the Darfur genocide, he has won an Emmy and several global humanitarian prizes. He has written six best-selling books, including the No. 1 best-seller Half the Sky and the memoir Chasing Hope, and has made several television documentaries. Kristof, who has lived on four continents and traveled to more than 160 countries, leads an annual fundraising appeal for selected nonprofits that now raises more than $50 million a year.If you have questions about accessibility or require accommodations to participate an event, please contact us at kdarling@berkeley.edu (mailto:kdarling@berkeley.edu) or call (510) 672-1869.

events.title: Catie Cuan // Physical AI: Giving AI a Robot Body
events.description: The Jacobs Institute for Design Innovation welcomes Dr. Catie Cuan, entrepreneur, engineer, artist, and pioneer in the emerging field of choreorobotics. Working at the intersection of artificial intelligence, robotics, and human-robot interaction, Catie explores how movement shapes the way we perceive and relate to machines. She is the founder of ART Lab (AI Robot Technology), and has led work across institutions including Stanford University and the Exploratorium, where she served as artist in residence. ​In her talk, Physical AI: Giving AI a Robot Body, Catie will explore what happens as AI moves beyond screens and into the physical world. As robots become more intelligent, how they move becomes just as important as what they can do. Drawing on her unique background in dance and robotics, she argues that movement is not just functional, but expressive, shaping emotion, trust, and human connection. Through examples from her work, including training robots to improvise, respond to human gestures, and move collectively, she will show how choreography can inform the design of more intuitive, responsive, and human-centered machines. ​Come experience a glimpse of a future where robots do not just act intelligently, but move with intention, awareness, and a sense of presence that changes how we live alongside them. ​This event is free and open to the public. ……………….. ​Design Field Notes (https://jacobsinstitute.berkeley.edu/design-field-notes/?utm_source=luma) is a lecture series where we invite the public to the UC Berkeley campus for conversations with designers, makers and artists who are contributing to shaping the future through design.If you require accommodation for a disability for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Jacobs Institute staff atjacobsinstitute@berkeley.edu (mailto:jacobsinstitute@berkeley.edu)with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: Applied Math Seminar: Foundational Research in the Age of AI
events.description: Speaker: Tammy Kolda, MathSci.aiWhat are the *actual* capabilities of AI in research, especially for foundational research, stripped of hype? I'll talk about independent evaluations on math research problems from First Proof (born in Berkeley!). I'll spend some time on how AI actually works, considering a functional view of what LLMs are. I'll also discuss the mounting stresses on scholarly publishing. The impact of AI on research could go many ways, and we as a field have some control over this. Part of the answer might me more independent assessments, so that the view of the AI companies doesn't dominate. My wish is for foundational research to be grander than today, valuing fewer, higher-quality contributions (versus easily generated quantity), and motivated by intense curiosity and passion. But this is just the beginning of the discussion!

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with David Henkin
events.description: In Out of the Ballpark (Oxford, 2026), David Henkin (History) reconsiders the character, meaning, and delights of baseball by exploring the game's unusual features and the sport's many resonances with other aspects of modern life. To this end, he abandons several assumptions and mythologies that underlie most approaches to histories of baseball: that it is unique among sports and fundamentally different from other kinds of entertainment; that it is specific to the United States; that it has changed fundamentally in recent years; and that the keys to understanding it lie primarily in examining what happens on the field of play. Instead, Henkin moves across time and space to examine baseball's history since the nineteenth century and beyond US borders. He takes readers inside the structures of clubs and leagues, interprets the sacred scripture of rulebooks, and illuminates some of baseball's rites and rituals that are often associated with honor and manhood. He charts baseball's significance along the routes of American and Japanese imperial expansion and the shifting maps of race and ethnicity in the US. Baseball is found at negotiating tables that pit capital against labor and in pivotal moments in the history of mass media. He shows us how baseball might offer a complex and capacious space for thinking about such things as spectatorship, success, community, order, and contingency in the modern world. Henkin is joined by Alva Noë (Philosophy). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: Bioengineering Seminar: Activity-Based Assays for Monitoring Treatment and Prevention of Infectious Diseases
events.description: Abstract: For many infectious and chronic diseases, effective medications already exist, and prevention or treatment succeeds or fails on whether those drugs are dosed and taken correctly. Concentrations that are too low lead to new infection or treatment failure, and concentrations that are too high cause adverse reactions. Current methods for measuring drug concentrations are expensive, labor-intensive, and slow, which puts them out of reach for most people who would benefit from them. Rapid and inexpensive tests would make monitoring and dose individualization far more widely available, from centralized laboratories to the bedside and the home, and particularly in resource-limited settings. Our lab develops tests that measure drug concentrations using the drugs' own biochemical activity rather than by detecting the drug molecules themselves. We have built user-friendly tests that measure the active intracellular forms of several human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) medications, with excellent concordance with gold-standard mass spectrometry. We extended this approach to therapeutic drug monitoring of cytomegalovirus (CMV) medications, measuring ganciclovir triphosphate in infants with congenital CMV, where dosing must avoid both underexposure and toxicity. The same need applies to transplant recipients and other immunocompromised populations. Most recently, we inverted our assay principle: by measuring the activity of reverse transcriptase derived from patient samples, rather than recombinant enzyme, we can measure HIV viral load and detect phenotypic drug resistance in the same rapid and user-friendly format. Our current focus is on optimizing, validating, and delivering these tests to populations in need both locally and globally, building a unified toolkit for monitoring drug exposure, viral suppression, and drug resistance at the point of need.

events.title: Camilla Maiani | Marie Curie (1867-1934): The Making of a Myth
events.description: Marie Curie is one of the most famous scientists in modern history. She is especially celebrated for her pioneering work on radioactivity, and for being the only person to have received two Nobel prizes, in Physics and in Chemistry. Over time, she has also become an iconic figure for feminists and women in science. But behind the myth lies a much more complex figure, firmly rooted in the social and cultural context of her time. This conference explores Marie Curie's scientific achievements, while examining how her public image was shaped during her lifetime - particularly during her first official visit to the United States - and how it continued to change after her death in 1934. Camilla Maiani has a PhD and a background in particle physics research and has worked at the CEA and the Université d'Orsay in collaboration with the CERN laboratories in Geneva. Today, she is a science and science history outreach specialist at the Curie Museum in Paris, where she develops educational content based on the museum's collections. events.title: CTML Seminar Series: Tianyue Zhou (CTML GSR)
events.description: This week's seminar brings another thought-provoking discussion! Join us on October 28th to hear from CTML GSR Tianyue Zhou (https://ctml.berkeley.edu/people/tianyue-zhou) presenting his talk on "A CV-TMLE Global Test Approach to Improve Power in Rare Disease Clinical Studies with Multiple-Component Endpoints." The seminar will take place at 12:00 PM in Berkeley Way West, 5th Floor, Room 5401.Abstract: Rare disease trials face unique statistical challenges due to limited patient populations and heterogeneous clinical manifestations among patients. Multiple endpoints are often necessary to comprehensively capture treatment benefits. A global test is an approach for evaluating whether a treatment has any beneficial effect across multiple endpoints. We propose a new global test based on a weighted composite endpoint. The proposed global test employs shrinkage-based cross-validated targeted maximum likelihood estimation (CV-TMLE) to learn data-adaptive weights that maximize power while maintaining Type I error control. Shrinkage can be tailored to incorporate existing domain knowledge, such as anticipated relative effect sizes. In simulation studies designed to reflect real rare disease trial settings, the proposed procedure demonstrated improved power over standard multiplicity adjustments and classical global tests (such as the O'Brien test), while maintaining nominal Type I error, when effects are heterogeneous across endpoints. The proposed method simultaneously learns an optimal weighted composite outcome and provides an unbiased and efficient targeted maximum likelihood estimator (TMLE) for the average treatment effect (ATE) on that weighted outcome, with valid inference taking into account that the ATE is data dependent.Bio: Tianyue Zhou is currently a PhD student in Biostatistics at the University of California, Berkeley, working with Mark van der Laan and Maya Petersen. His research interests primarily lie in the intersection of causal inference and machine learning, with a focus on real-world evidence generation and improving efficiency in randomized trials.

events.title: Jeffrey Bowers: Research in NeuroAI should focus more on the findings and methods of psychology to advance our understanding of biological intelligence
events.description: The dual quests – to understand intelligence as it arises in biology and to build it in machines of our own making – have been with us for nearly a century. While neuroscience and psychology seek to characterize intelligence in terms of underlying neural mechanisms and emergent behavior, we still lack a set of principles that can account for how the interactions of many neurons within a brain give rise to intelligent behavior. Meanwhile, modern AI is following a largely empirical path to create a new technology without scientific foundation. While the resulting algorithms exhibit intriguing behavior, the working principles are unknown, usage risks are incalculable, and the path to further development is unclear. The premise of this seminar is that the current century will see the emergence of a new scientific discipline – the Science of Intelligence – that seeks to elucidate universal principles that govern intelligent systems, be they biological or machine, and that this will provide both much needed insight in neuroscience and a solid foundation for technological development. The seminar will meet weekly, featuring speakers from across campus and elsewhere, who will share their views on the open questions, topics of study and debate, and relevant disciplines that a science of intelligence will encompass. Wednesday, October 28, 2026 Time: 12:00pm Location: 101 Weill Hall Speaker: Jeffrey Bowers (https://jeffbowers.blogs.bristol.ac.uk/) Affiliation: University of Bristol (https://www.bristol.ac.uk/psychology-neuroscience/)

events.title: PMB Seminar with Brian D. Gregory | RNA cleavage-mediated post-transcriptional regulation of the plant transcriptome
events.description: RNA cleavage is essential for processing and regulating all classes of RNA. Current methods profiling genome-wide RNA cleavage are biased towards cytoplasmic events and ignore compartmentalized differences. We have recently coupled subcellular RNA fractionation with degradome profiling to detect genome-wide nucleoplasm- and cytoplasm-enriched RNA cleavage in Arabidopsis thaliana. Using this enhanced profiling data we are studying RNA processing, including microRNAs, as well as RNA modification-mediated effects of RNA cleavage-mediated post-transcriptional regulation of the plant transcriptome. Our most recent results on miRNA processing and RNA modification-mediated regulation of the plant transcriptome will be presented.

events.title: Traces on the Landscape - Humboldt's Journey in Peru's Far North: 1802 & Today
events.description: This talk will take place in person at the ARF. Abstract: Alexander von Humboldt, a highly-educated and enthusiastic 29-year-old Prussian aristocrat bent on adventure, set sail from Spain in 1799 on a five-year journey of scientific exploration in America's Spanish colonies. With permission from the King of Spain, and self-financed, he aimed to "find out about the unity of nature" as he wrote to a friend on the eve of departure. Over the ensuing five years, and with his traveling companion French botanist Aime Bonpland, they collected over 5,000 plant specimens, while Humboldt himself measured everything he could, amassing a vast amount of data on oceanography, climate, geology, magnetism and plant distributions, among other subjects. In his travel diaries he included notes on political economy, and peoples and places in the waning years of colonial rule. He was fascinated by what had preceded the Spanish and he measured and sketched the remains of Inca structures along the way. Returning to Europe he published dozens of works, both scientific and popular. Celebrated as the most famous scientist, public intellectual and humanist in the 19th century, he inspired Charles Darwin to embark on the Beagle, and in the United States he had a major influence on John Muir, and on writers including Thoreau, Emerson and Whitman as he was laying the foundations for the field of biogeography and the science of ecology. In her talk Sandra Nichols will focus on a little-known segment of Humboldt's five year journey during the month of August 1802 when he traveled by mule train along the spine of the Andes, and descended by balsa raft to the Marañón river, a major tributary of the Amazon. Today it's virtually unknown territory for most Peruvians, and understudied by scholars. Humboldt himself never wrote up a full account of his travels in the region, but drawing on his recently discovered travel diaries, along with archival research and exploratory visits with Peruvian colleagues to multiple sites over the last ten years, she will discuss the region's unique geographic features, contemporary threats to its natural resources, alongside its cultural heritage that dates back at least 5,000 BP. About the Speaker: Sandra Nichols grew up in Lima, Peru where everyone learned about the "La Corriente de Humboldt," but knew nothing about the man. On returning to the U.S. for college she earned a BA in Anthropology and MA in Communication, both from Stanford. Following a 20+ year career producing documentary films, primarily in Asia and Africa, and for broadcast on Public Television, including the NOVA Series, she returned to academia and earned a PhD in Berkeley's Geography Department in 2002. Her dissertation focus was transnational communities and labor migration between Mexico and California, but on the side she was developing a fascination for Humboldt, picking up his trail in Mexico, in Europe, in the U.S. and, since 2016, chasing after him in Peru. This talk draws from sections of a book she is writing to be published in 2027 for a Peruvian audience, and in Spanish, titled: Alexander von Humboldt: Caminos y Encuentros – Un viaje en el norte del Peru. Her book collaborators include photographer Heinz Plenge Pardo, graphic artist Sandra Zimic.Image credit: Heinz Plenge Pardo

events.title: The Quest for Identity and Agency as a Black Scholar and Human Rights Activist with Charles P. Henry
events.description: Please RSVP to attend (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSd9zDNbTjwYPyhYmiy4l5A4krh_J6d-zqwh4narTg7HYeIKVg/viewform?usp=dialog). Join us for a conversation with Professor Emeritus Charles Henry about his new memoir, The Quest for Identity and Agency as a Black Scholar and Human Rights Activist (https://www.amazon.com/dp/1917503091?lv=shuf&channelId=500&plpRedirect=mhFallback). In this compelling book, Professor Charles P. Henry explores his involvement in two pivotal social movements: the search for social identity and the fight for civil and human rights. Starting with personal experiences of place, memory, family, Black Studies, and reparations, Henry's narrative expands to broader issues like the Black diaspora, global community, and intersectionality.Charles P. Henry, is Professor Emeritus of African American Studies at the University of California at Berkeley. In 1994, President Clinton appointed him to the National Council on the Humanities for a six-year term. Former president of the National Council for Black Studies, Henry is the author/editor of ten books and more than 80 articles and reviews on Black politics, public policy, and human rights. Before joining the University of California at Berkeley in 1981, Henry taught at Denison University and Howard University. Henry was chair of the board of directors of Amnesty International U.S.A. from 1986 to 1988 and is a former NEH Post-doctoral Fellow and American Political Science Association Congressional Fellow. In 1994-95 he served as an office director in the Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor at the U.S. Department of State. Professor Henry was Distinguished Fulbright Chair in American History and Politics at the University of Bologna, Italy for the Spring semester of 2003. In the fall of 2006, Henry was one of the first two Fulbright-Tocqueville Distinguished Chairs in France teaching at the University of Tours. Chancellor Birgeneau presented Henry with the Chancellor's Award for Advancing Institutional Excellence in April 2008. Henry was Chair of the Board of the Center for Victims of Torture from 2023 to 2025. He holds a doctorate in Political Science from the University of Chicago. In his retirement, Professor Henry is a regular food bank volunteer.

events.title: Trauma-Informed Client Intake Skills Workshop
events.description: This skills-based workshop will introduce law students to trauma-informed approaches for conducting client intakes in legal settings. The workshop will be facilitated by Arati Vasan (Family Violence Appellate Project) and Orchid Pusey (Asian Women's Shelter). Students will learn practical techniques for creating a safe, respectful, and supportive environment while gathering the information necessary to assess a client's legal needs. Through interactive exercises and simulated client interviews, students will practice trauma-informed communication, active listening, and strategies for responding to sensitive or difficult disclosures. The workshop will also address how trauma can affect memory, communication, trust, and decision-making during the intake process. By the end of the workshop, students will have concrete tools for conducting client intakes that are both legally effective and responsive to the experiences and needs of clients.The skills taught in this workshop are broadly applicable across legal practice areas and client populations, including domestic violence, immigration, housing, family law, and even big law. events.title: Spectral Theory Seminar: A sharp lower bound on the small eigenvalues of surfaces
events.description: Speaker: Asaf Nachmias, Tel Aviv University, visiting Simons InstituteLet S be a compact hyperbolic surface of genus g1. We prove that for any k in {1,...,2g-3} the k-th eigenvalue of the Laplacian is at least ck^2/(g^2 I(S)) where c is a universal constant, I(S) is the average of 1/max(Inj(x)^2,1) over x in S, and Inj(x) is the injectivity radius at x. This bound is optimal in the sense that for every g1 there exists a compact hyperbolic surface of genus g satisfying the reverse inequality with a different universal constant. Joint work with Renan Gross and Guy Lachman.

events.title: Probability Seminar: Maximillian Newman "Rigidity of infinite exchangeable sequences"
events.description: Abstract: In recent works, it has been shown that infinite exchangeable sequences with Gaussian marginals have remarkable rigidity properties, namely that Gaussianity of just the first two elements of the sequence implies the whole sequence is Gaussian. I will present the general case of mixture kernels and demonstrate that an analogous result holds, namely that the distribution of the first three elements of the sequence determines the full law of the sequence under a Muntz-Szasz type criterion. These results strengthen results in non-parametric identifiability of mixtures and yield sharp finite-dimensional refinements of classical theorem of Freedman.

events.title: Geography Colloquia Series - All that is compute transforms into concrete: Monopoly rent and the fixity of AI's infrastructure
events.description: In the capitalist imaginary, artificial intelligence is narrated on dematerialization. In this telling, capital has escaped the weight of human labor via the frictionless circulation of data. This paper argues the opposite: the AI economy is a geography of fixity, where training large language models requires warehouse-scale data centers anchored to specific territories by the demands of energy, infrastructure, and available land. Two analytical categories theorize this fixity. The first concerns the monopoly control of location and network proximity: value is extracted from whoever sits closest to the data, controls the interconnection, and commands the lowest latency. The second concerns the monopoly control of computation itself: training frontier AI models is capital-intensive, technically scarce, and concentrated in a handful of firms who can extract a tribute that is not reducible to productivity but to infra/structural position. Both forms of extraction are rent. And both are responses to a profitability crisis in the AI sector driven by rising fixed capital requirements that outpace returns. We draw on financial filings, industry reports, and field observations in Northern Virginia's Data Center Alley to show that what appears as an agglomeration economy is better understood as rent extracted through the strategic fixity of capital in digital infrastructure. Dillon Mahmoudi (dillonm@umbc.edu) is an Associate Professor of Geography and Environmental Systems at the University of Maryland Baltimore County. and Alan Wiig (alanwiig@ufl.edu) is an Associate Professor of Geography at the University of Florida. They recently published a book chapter, Land for AI: Data Center Real Estate Markets in The Inner World of Artificial Intelligence (2026).

events.title: Matrix on Point: The State of U.S. Immigration Enforcement and Surveillance
events.description: REGISTER Federal immigration enforcement in the United States is increasingly shaped by the convergence of surveillance technologies, data systems, and on-the-ground policing practices. From AI-assisted identification tools to information-sharing across agencies, these developments are transforming how enforcement operates, and raising urgent questions about civil liberties and democratic oversight. This panel will bring together scholars to examine the social and political consequences, and the stakes for rights in an era of technological governance. The panel will feature David Hausman, Assistant Professor at UC Berkeley Law School, Caitlin Patler, Associate Professor of Public Policy at the UC Berkeley Goldman School of Public Policy, and Jennifer Urban, Clinical Professor of Law at UC Berkeley Law School. Deirdre Mulligan, Professor in the UC Berkeley School of Information, will moderate. This event is co-sponsored by the Asian American Research Center, the Center for Race and Gender, the Berkeley Interdisciplinary Migration Initiative, the Goldman School of Public Policy, and the UC Berkeley School of Information.Matrix On Point (https://matrix.berkeley.edu/category/event-type/matrix-on-point/) is a discussion series promoting focused, cross-disciplinary conversations on today's most pressing issues. Offering opportunities for scholarly exchange and interaction, each Matrix On Point features the perspectives of leading scholars and specialists from different disciplines, followed by an open conversation. These thought-provoking events are free and open to the public. Panelists David Hausman (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/our-faculty/faculty-profiles/david-hausman/#tab_profile) is an Assistant Professor at Berkeley Law School. He does empirical work on U.S. immigration enforcement, mostly using government data disclosed in response to Freedom of Information Act requests. He also co-directs the Deportation Data Project (https://deportationdata.org/). Before joining Berkeley, he practiced law at the ACLU Immigrants' Rights Project in New York City.Caitlin Patler (https://gspp.berkeley.edu/research-and-impact/faculty/caitlin-patler) is Associate Professor of Public Policy at the UC Berkeley Goldman School of Public Policy, and faculty affiliate of the Berkeley Interdisciplinary Migration Initiative (BIMI), Berkeley Population Center, and the Institute for Research on Labor and Employment. Dr. Patler's research examines US immigration and criminal laws, legal statuses, and law enforcement institutions as drivers of socioeconomic and health disparities.Jennifer M. Urban (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/our-faculty/faculty-profiles/jennifer-urban/#tab_profile) is a Clinical Professor of Law at UC Berkeley School of Law, where she is Director of Policy Initiatives at the Samuelson Law, Technology & Public Policy Clinic (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/experiential/clinics/samuelson-law-technology-public-policy-clinic/). Her research focuses on information policy: intellectual property, privacy and data protection, and security. She regularly collaborates with technologists and academics in disciplines other than law to develop empirically grounded understandings of how new technologies and the regulatory structures around them interact with civil liberties, innovation, and creative expression. In March 2021, Urban was appointed by California Governor Gavin Newsom to be the inaugural Chair of the California Privacy Protection Agency Board.Deirdre K. Mulligan (https://www.ischool.berkeley.edu/people/deirdre-mulligan) (moderator) is a Professor in the School of Information at UC Berkeley, a faculty Director of the Berkeley Center for Law & Technology (https://www.law.berkeley.edu/research/bclt/), and a co-organizer of the Algorithmic Fairness & Opacity Working Group (http://afog.berkeley.edu/). Mulligan's research explores legal and technical means of protecting values such as privacy, freedom of expression, and fairness in socio-technical systems. Her book Privacy on the Ground: Driving Corporate Behavior in the United States and Europe (https://mitpress.mit.edu/books/privacy-ground), a study of privacy practices in large corporations in five countries, with UC Berkeley Law Prof. Kenneth Bamberger was published in 2015 by MIT Press. Mulligan served as Principal Deputy U.S. Chief Technology Officer at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, (https://www.whitehouse.gov/ostp/) and Director of the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Office (NAIIO), in the Biden-Harris Administration. In November 2025, Mulligan was appointed to Governor Newsom's California Innovation Council. REGISTER

events.title: EECS Colloquium: Compiler 2.0: Building the Next Generation of Compilers with Machine Learning
events.description: The genius of FORTRAN, introduced in 1957, was not just that it was the first widely successful high-level language, but that it made hardware disappear. The same FORTRAN program could run on an IBM System/360, a DEC PDP-8, a CDC 6600, or even a Cray-1, with enough performance that most programmers never had to touch assembly or write architecture-specific code. Over time, as both hardware and software grew more complex, compilers quietly lost much of their ability to maintain this abstraction. Multicores, complex vector instructions, and specialized accelerators have pushed more of the performance burden back onto the programmer. Today, we have, in many ways, come full circle. For example, getting peak performance from NVIDIA's V100, A100, H100, and B100 generations often requires different, architecture-specific CUDA kernels and, on the latest parts, even hand-written PTX assembly to fully exploit tensor cores and the Tensor Memory Accelerator. To the best of our knowledge, the Apple/Arm SME accelerator does not even have a high-level compiler, and most high-performance code must be written using intrinsics or assembly. The recent AI revolution is bringing capabilities that are poised to upend the traditional compiler. Machine learning can give existing compilers capabilities they have never had, from making complex optimization decisions to generating substantial portions of compiler passes. At the extreme, LLMs may replace much of the traditional compiler as we know it. This raises a fundamental question: can the next generation of compilers finally fulfill the promise that began with FORTRAN? Can they transform a single, high-level description of an algorithm into light-speed implementations across CPUs, GPUs, and specialized accelerators, while once again making the underlying hardware disappear? In this talk, I will hallucinate about this exciting possibility, drawing lessons from the history of compiler research and exploring possible paths toward building Compiler 2.0. Saman Amarasinghe is the Thomas and Gerd Perkins Professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and a member of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), where he leads the Commit Compiler Research Group. Under his leadership, the Commit group has developed a wide range of innovative programming languages and compilers, including StreamIt, StreamJIT, PetaBricks, Halide, TACO, Finch, SySTeC, GraphIt, Simit, MILK, Cimple, BioStream, NetBlocks, BREeze, CoLa, Shim, AskIt, and Seq. Additionally, the group has created compiler and runtime frameworks such as DynamoRIO, Helium, Tiramisu, Codon, BuildIt, and D2X, as well as vectorization techniques and tools such as Superword Level Parallelism (SLP), goSLP, and VeGen. Saman's team also developed Ithemal, a machine-learning-based performance predictor; Program Shepherding, which protects programs from external attacks; the extensible OpenTuner autotuning framework; and Kendo, a deterministic execution system. He co-led the Raw architecture project. Outside academia, Saman has founded or co-founded several companies, including Determina, Lanka Internet Services Ltd., Venti Technologies, DataCebo, Exaloop, and Build4Sim. He earned his BS in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science from Cornell University in 1988, and his MSEE and Ph.D. from Stanford University in 1990 and 1997, respectively. He is a Fellow of the ACM and a recipient of the ACM-IEEE CS Ken Kennedy Award.

events.title: MBN Seminar: Leveraging Big Data from Human Cohorts to Reveal the Biology of Thermogenic Fat
events.description: Paul Cohen, M.D., Ph.D., Albert Resnick,M.D. Associate Professor, Head, Weslie R. and William H. Janeway Laboratory of Molecular Metabolism, The Rockefeller UniversityTitle: Leveraging Big Data from Human Cohorts to Reveal the Biology of Thermogenic FatSummary: Over 2 billion adults worldwide are overweight or obese, and excess body weight significantly increases the risk of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, cardiovascular disease, and many types of cancer. Little is known about how obesity contributes to the pathogenesis of these diseases, which in aggregate are the leading causes of morbidity and mortality in much of the world. My laboratory focuses on understanding how obesity leads to metabolic diseases and cancer with the ultimate goal of developing therapies to break the link between them. Obesity is defined by excess white fat, which contributes to associated diseases, but mammals also possess brown fat, which can convert chemical energy into heat. We have contributed to a fundamental understanding of molecular and tissue-level regulation of brown fat, but this tissue was long thought to have a limited role in human physiology. We have used a large patient cohort study to show that brown fat is in fact associated with significant metabolic and cardiovascular health benefits. My research program investigates the biology and genetics of brown fat to understand how it mediates these pleiotropic effects. Centered on human biology and employing unique patient cohorts and novel imaging and biochemical methods, we take a systems-based approach to dissect the role of brown fat in health and disease.

events.title: Neyman Statistics Seminar with Yizhe Zhu: Differentially private synthetic data generation
events.description: Abstract: Differentially private synthetic data enables the sharing and analysis of sensitive datasets while providing rigorous privacy guarantees for individual contributors. A central challenge is to preserve the information needed for meaningful downstream analysis. Many existing methods aim to preserve a broad range of statistical properties, but their accuracy can deteriorate as the number of variables grows. This motivates approaches that exploit structure in the data and in the statistical questions of interest. In this talk, I will present a sequence of works on efficient private synthetic data generation and explain how low-dimensional data structure and smoothness in the statistical quantities of interest can yield improved accuracy with nearly optimal guarantees. I will also introduce a general moment-matching framework for constructing private synthetic data tailored to the chosen class of queries. Bio: Yizhe Zhu is an Assistant Professor of Mathematics at the University of Southern California. His research lies at the intersection of probability and mathematical data science, with an emphasis on random matrices and tensors, high-dimensional inference, and differential privacy. Before joining USC, he was a Visiting Assistant Professor at the University of California, Irvine, and a postdoctoral fellow at the Simons Laufer Mathematical Sciences Institute in Berkeley. He earned his Ph.D. in Mathematics from the University of California, San Diego, in 2021.

events.title: Combinatorics Seminar: From tangent bundles of matroids to a stone game
events.description: Speaker: JungTao (Ronnie) Cheng, Stanford UniversityThe Hodge theory of matroids illustrates how geometric ideas can lead to combinatorial results. In this talk, I will introduce a tangent class for a matroid and explain how it provides a matroidal Riemann–Roch formula. I will then discuss a numerical Kawamata–Viehweg vanishing theorem for rank-three matroids and explain how it reduces to an inequality for a stone game. Time permitting, I will give a combinatorial proof and the geometric insights behind the argument.

events.title: Laura Sánchez Carrasco & Íñigo Cobeta: What Space Builds | Architecture Lecture Series
events.description: Laura Sánchez Carrasco is an architect and associate professor at the Escuela Técnica Superior de Arquitectura, UPM, where she has taught since 2018. She holds a degree in architecture (2007), a master's in analysis, theory, and history of architecture (2014), and a PhD cum laude (2017), all from UPM. Her research addresses postwar North American architecture and its connections with Spanish architecture, combining architectural history with digital methods of historiographic analysis. She is currently part of the research project "Conexiones de la arquitectura española con las Américas (1976–2006)" and has previously collaborated with MIT on the project "Mapping Global Architectural Histories on Modernism". Alongside her academic career, she practiced architecture professionally for nearly 20 years, both running her own studio and working within established firms, where she led competition-winning projects from design through construction. Íñigo Cobeta is a researcher and associate professor in the Department of Architectural Composition at the Escuela Técnica Superior de Arquitectura de Madrid (ETSAM), where he has taught since 2006. He has collaborated with specialized international publications such as ArquitecturaCOAM or RITA. He has also acted as an independent national curator (Bienal Iberoamericana de Arquitectura y Urbanismo 2006). For 20 years he worked as an architect, collaborating with MoneoBrockStudio on the Termas de Tiberio in the Panticosa Spa and developing his own practice. In 2019, the bicentennial of the Museo Nacional del Prado, he was invited to lecture on some of the conclusions of his thesis, The Prado, from Territory to Stage, directed by Rafael Moneo. He is currently part of the research project "Conexiones de la arquitectura española con las Américas (1976–2006)". Since 2020, he has focused on teaching, research, and developing experimental projects on public schools.
