events.description: An Art, Technology, & Culture Colloquium lecture, presented as part of BCNM's Indigenous Technologies program, curated by Indigenous Technologies Coordinator Talia Dixon, co-sponsored by the Arts Practice Department, the Department of Theater, Dance, and Performance Studies, and the Graduate Students of Theater, Dance, and Performance Studies with Tanya Lukin Linklater Artist-Choreographer and Faculty Mentor, Institute of American Indian Arts - Monday, November 2, 2026 5:00 — 6:30 PM Eugene Jarvis Auditorium,Grimes Engineering Center (http://engineering.berkeley.edu/about/facilities/grimes-engineering-center/) RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLScK01nSupvyyNJV1xSGzG8Gol7h0iXJEiqUM9ucuwBhNkMCuA/viewform?usp=publish-editor)! Save the event to your bCal here (https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?action=TEMPLATE&tmeid=N3FoYm1uYWs0b25vb2FnazZyaDcybWhxNzYgZDV1NWVrN2o4aXBvZDBvOGlxNDE1ZTFhdnNAZw&tmsrc=d5u5ek7j8ipod0o8iq415e1avs%40group.calendar.google.com)! - Compelled by lineages of Sugpiaq cultural work and their continuance despite imperial and colonial disruptions of their lifeways, Tanya Lukin Linklater will discuss her ongoing practice of visiting ancestral belongings — Sugpiaq technologies — in museum collections, including UC Berkeley's Hearst Museum of Anthropology. The talk will then bring into focus her speculative responses to photographic documentation of Sugpiaq belongings in the Kunstkamera in St. Petersburg, Russia. Coupled with her meditations on estuaries, grasses, and customary practices of the Kodiak archipelago, these threads organize Crested, her solo exhibition at Portikus, Frankfurt, and Tendon thread, a performance commission for the Center for Human Rights and the Arts and Fisher Center at Bard College, premiering in winter 2026. Workshop Opportunity Tanya Lukin Linklater will also host an inclusive workshop for UC Berkeley students and community members that involves creative writing, embodied inquiry, and meditations on Sugpiaq grasses, the following afternoon, Tuesday, November 3, from 4:30 to 6:30 pm, at Bancroft Dance Studio (https://tdps.berkeley.edu/about/directions/bancroft). Participation is limited to 25 people, and registration requires completion of this brief questionnaire (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSf2zl8_3bpc7HPinRsBotpgW9yoCmahdgrUtbY6FTxiMKFRMg/viewform?usp=publish-editor). Participants will be reminded of workshop approximately one week prior. About Tanya Lukin Linklater Tanya Lukin Linklater makes dances in museums, videos, sculptures, and works on paper. She thinks with weather, embodiment, beingness, and ancestral belongings in her practice. She is compelled by scores, orality, poetics, embodied inquiry, Indigenous knowledge transmission, and ephemerality. Her recent and forthcoming exhibitions and performances include Camden Art Centre, London, UK; Dia Art Foundation, New York; National Gallery of Canada, Ottawa; Portikus, Frankfurt; Rudolfinum, Prague; SITE SANTA FE; and Fisher Center at Bard, Annandale-on-Hudson, New York. Her artworks have entered the collections of Agnes Etherington Art Centre, Art Gallery of Ontario, Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art, Remai Modern, San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, Tate Americas Foundation, Vancouver Art Gallery, Walker Art Center, and elsewhere. Her book, Slow Scrape (2nd edition, Talonbooks, Vancouver 2022), draws on documentary poetics, concrete-based installations, event scores, and can be read alongside her choreographic practice. Her recent publications include contributions to The Routledge Companion to Indigenous Art Histories in the United States and Canada, Jeffrey Gibson: the space in which to place me, Mark: Sonya Kelliher-Combs, and Native Visual Sovereignty: A Reader on Art and Performance. In 2024 she was awarded a post-doctoral fellowship in Decolonial and Transformational Indigenous Art Practices with Dr. Heather Igloliorte, Canada Excellence Research Chair, at University of Victoria. A dedicated educator, Tanya was a faculty mentor in the Institute of American Indian Arts' MFA in Studio Arts 2021-2026. About Indigenous Technologies Indigenous Technologies is a program of BCNM that engages questions of technology and new media in relation to global structures of indigeneity, settler colonialism, and genocide in the 21st century. Our Indigenous Tech events and ongoing conversations with Indigenous scholars and communities aim to critically envision and reimagine what a more just and sustainable technological future can look like. We highlight Indigenous engagements with robotics, computer science, telecommunications, artificial intelligence, virtual reality, social media, online activism, video games, and more.

events.title: Merck Symposium
events.description: Jim Morken, Professor & Louise and Jim Vanderslice and Family Chair, Boston CollegeMerck Symposium Flyer (https://events.berkeley.edu/live/files/72-merck-symposium-flyer)Catalytic Stereoselective Synthesis with Boron ReagentsChiral organoboronic esters are versatile intermediates for chemical synthesis. Not only are these compounds stable under a variety of reaction conditions, they are generally non-toxic and can be transformed with minimal generation of hazardous waste. An important feature of aliphatic organoboronic esters is that the boron atom may be replaced with an array of different functional groups through efficient, stereospecific transformations. This seminar will cover new strategies for the construction of alkylboronic esters from simple starting materials in a catalytic enantioselective fashion, and will also discuss ways in which these compounds can functionalized by catalytic stereospecific couplings. In addition, application of organoboronate-based transformations to address compelling problems in chemical synthesis will be discussed. Professor James Morken was born in Concord, California and obtained his B.S. in chemistry in 1989 from UC Santa Barbara working with Prof. Bruce Rickborn. He obtained his Ph.D. from Boston College in 1995 with Prof. Amir Hoveyda and was an NSF Postdoctoral Fellow with Stuart Schreiber at Harvard University. In 1997, he became an Assistant Professor of Chemistry at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. He was promoted to Associate Professor in 2002 and in 2006 joined the faculty of Boston College. In 2014, he was named the Louise and James Vanderslice and Family Chaired Professor of Chemistry at Boston College. Professor Morken's research focuses on the development of transition-metal-catalyzed asymmetric processes and their use in complex molecule synthesis. He is particularly interested in the study and development of catalytic enantioselective reactions involving organoboron reagents. Because of the broad array of reactions that available to organoboronates, these types of process can be employed to address a number of compelling problems in the construction of organic frameworks.

events.title: Kapil Ramachandran: Neuroproteasomes and the spatial control of neuronal proteostasis
events.description: Neurons must synthesize proteins at precise times, in response to external cues, and in compartments far from the cell body. Nascent proteins are particularly susceptible to misfolding, yet the mechanisms that rapidly monitor proteins made in dendrites remain poorly understood. We discovered a distinct population of proteasomes that appears to span the neuronal plasma membrane, where these "neuroproteasomes" degrade a subset of proteins during or immediately after translation. Despite evidence for neuroproteasomes across multiple systems, how they associate with the membrane, which proteins they select, and their functions in neurons remain largely unknown. I will argue that neuroproteasomes offer a new cell biological framework for the initiation of protein aggregation, while their constitutive activity converts intracellular proteolysis into extracellular neuromodulation.

events.title: Seminar 218, Psychology and Economics: Joshua Schwartzstein "Channeled Attention and Stable Errors"
events.description: Abstract: People persist in mistaken beliefs even in settings with high stakes, abundant data, and repeated opportunities to learn—settings where standard arguments imply they should correct their errors. We develop an attention-based framework for understanding why errors persist. When a person channels his attention through the lens of his potentially misspecified model, exposure to data is not the same as tracking the statistics necessary to tell him his model is wrong. A model is attentionally stable when the data the person deems relevant fail, in the long run, to make the model look implausible. Models that erroneously rule things out—e.g., beliefs that a variable doesn't matter or that a distinction doesn't exist—tend to be attentionally stable because they divert attention away from data that would refute the model. Conversely, models that erroneously rule things in are less likely to be stable. Whether an error is discovered depends on the structure of the decision problem but is not tightly linked to its stakes; arbitrarily costly errors can persist while trivially inexpensive ones may be detected. Nevertheless, no error is robust both to changes in the decision environment and to shocks that expand attention: every channeled-attention error is vulnerable to some perturbation that would reveal it. We use the framework to analyze the stability of psychological biases and empirical misconceptions, as well as to explain why fresh eyes catch mistakes, why people use overly coarse rather than overly fine categorizations, and why people recognize errors in others that they miss in themselves. Paper Link: https://gagnon-bartsch.com/files/ChanneledAttention2026.pdf

events.title: Harold S. Johnston Lecture
events.description: Steven Brown, Deputy Director, NOAA Chemical Sciences LaboratoryPyrogenic Skies: Photochemistry, heterogeneous chemistry and air quality impacts of wildfire smoke As wildfires have increased in frequency and intensity across North America, their emissions have become a driver of regional air quality degradation. Biomass burning is a large source of ozone precursors, nitrogen oxides (NOx) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs), as well as particulate matter that impacts air quality directly and also drives heterogeneous chemical processes. Photochemistry within smoke plumes creates pyrogenic ozone over a variety of timescales, leading to short- and long-range transport and widespread increases in the ozone background. Mixing and entrainment of smoke that is rich in pyrogenic VOCs into NOx-rich urban areas alters regional photochemistry and can further enhance ozone production. However, aerosol loads associated with smoke layers may also suppress photochemistry. Heterogeneous chemistry in smoke plumes influences atmospheric composition through a different set of chemical cycles that affect both the lower and upper atmosphere. A series of recent airborne and ground-based field studies has investigated these chemical processes in biomass burning influenced air. These include the 2019 Fire Influence on Regional to Global Environments and Air Quality (FIREX-AQ), the 2022 California Fire Dynamics Experiment (CalFiDE), the 2023 Atmospheric Emissions and Reactivity Observed from Megacities to Marine Areas (AEROMMA) campaign, the 2024 Utah Summer Ozone study, and others. These studies provide new insights into the biomass burning influence on tropospheric ozone at all scales, from near field plume chemistry to the global remote troposphere, and from the continental background to local urban influence.

events.title: Fueling Patriarchy: Coal and Gender in the Upper Silesian Cultural Imagination
events.description: As the material foundation of industrialization, coal shaped not only economic processes but also social orders and cultural imaginaries in Central Europe – nowhere more visibly than in Upper Silesia, where coal's materiality helped generate a gendered division of labor: men worked below ground as active providers, women remained above ground in domestic, passive roles. Coal did not merely accompany this patriarchal gender order; it materially produced and sustained it. Drawing on energy humanities and feminist resource theory – most notably Cara Daggett's concept of petromasculinity – this talk traces how this coal-based gender matrix was consolidated, reproduced, and eventually destabilized in Upper Silesian literature, film, and performance from the early twentieth to the twenty-first century. Beginning with early twentieth-century literary representations, I show how cultural production consolidated a patriarchal, heteronormative matrix marked by hypermasculinity and the marginalization of women – a matrix that persisted through socialist realism and postsocialist transformation despite shifting political contexts. Only with the gradual closure of Upper Silesia's coal mines amid Poland's and the Czech Republic's energy transitions in the twenty-first century does a break emerge with this symbolic order: as coal's material grip loosens, so too does the heteronormative order it once underwrote. At the same time, cultural representation takes on a new discursive role, shifting from an instrument consolidating heteronormative codes into a space for renegotiating them. This becomes visible, for instance, in the Netflix series Królowa (2022) and in the drag and burlesque performances of the artistic-research collective Śląsk Przegięty, both of which recast coal and queerness not as opposites but as entangled parts of the region's identity. The talk aims to uncover the entanglements of coal and gender in Upper Silesia, showing how, as coal itself recedes, cultural representation becomes the space where its gender legacies are contested, undone, and reimagined.

events.title: Stefanie Hutka // What Your Machines Should Do: The Science and Strategy of Human-Centered Automation
events.description: The Jacobs Institute for Design Innovation welcomes Stefanie Hutka, design leader and author ofWhat Your Machines Should Do: The Science and Strategy of Human-Centered Automation. Stefanie has spent her career asking a question that sounds simple until you try to answer it: what should automation actually do, and for whom? ​Her talk centers on what she calls the "Automation Strategy Gap," the yawning distance between an organization's AI ambitions and its actual readiness to do something useful with them. It is, she argues, alarmingly wide. Drawing on human factors, cognitive science, and management theory, her book makes the case that AI is the latest chapter in a long history of automation, and that the durable lessons were always there, we just got distracted by the hype. One particularly useful provocation: automation accelerates the system you already have. Which means the first thing worth mapping is the beliefs driving your organization before you automate anything at all. ​This is a book launch talk. It will be an essential conversation for anyone who has sat through a roadmap presentation where "AI-powered" was doing a lot of heavy lifting where a strategy should have been. This event is free and open to the public. ……………….. ​Design Field Notes (https://jacobsinstitute.berkeley.edu/design-field-notes/?utm_source=luma) is a lecture series where we invite the public to the UC Berkeley campus for conversations with designers, makers and artists who are contributing to shaping the future through design.If you require accommodation for a disability for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact Jacobs Institute staff atjacobsinstitute@berkeley.edu (mailto:jacobsinstitute@berkeley.edu)with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Atreyee Gupta
events.description: Atreyee Gupta takes a revelatory look at modernism in India, exploring art's role in decolonization and aesthetic discourse across the Global South. Modernism's peak in the interwar and postwar decades coincided with the eruption of antifascist and decolonization movements globally, including the League against Imperialism, the Bandung Asian-African Conference, and the Non-Aligned Movement. Viewing artistic practices through the lens of the radical intellectual possibilities that these epoch-making events prompted, Atreyee Gupta (History of Art) uncovers a modernist internationalism incongruous with Westernist cultural hegemonies. Modernism, she shows, cannot be separated from concepts of freedom and autonomy generated by Third World political struggles. Gupta mobilizes concepts including liberation, anti-imperialism, development, and modernization as essential analytic categories for art history, reorienting our understanding of both global modernism and Indian art. Intertwining stories of art and liberation, aesthetics and decolonization, and intellectual practices and political revolution in the Third World, or what is now known as the Global South, Non-Aligned (Yale, 2025) follows the far-flung interwar and postwar networks in which Indian artists and intellectuals such as Francis N. Souza, Abanindranath and Gaganendranath Tagore, and Jagdish Swaminathan participated alongside interlocutors like W. E. B. Du Bois, Richard Wright, Octavio Paz, André Malraux, and Le Corbusier in Asia, Africa, Europe, and the Americas.

events.title: Italian Lives, Belgian Coal An Environmental History of Labor and Migration
events.description: On June 23, 1946, Italy and Belgium signed the "men in exchange for coal" agreement, in which Italy committed to sending fifty thousand workers each year to the Belgian coal mines, and Belgium pledged to supply a few thousand tons of coal to Italy each month. The first treaty of its kind, the agreement paved the way for the European Coal and Steel Community, a precursor of the European Union. In Italian Lives, Belgian Coal, Daniele Valisena explores the relationship between labor migration, coal extraction, and environmental transformation in the Belgian coalfields of Wallonia. Drawing from French, Italian, and Belgian archival documents; printed primary sources; and oral history interviews conducted by the author, this book breaks new methodological and empirical ground, blending environmental history and the history of migration, historical literature and anthropological work, and history and the contemporary. Each chapter captures and interrogates the agency of different actors, including the Italian and Belgian states, the coal industry, medical experts, miners, and the ecologies that develop in polluted areas left by the coal industry. Italian Lives, Belgian Coal tells a sobering story of the environmental and corporeal injustice wielded by capitalist institutions and its impact on health and medical science, society, and nature.Daniele Valisena, Visiting Fellow, German Historical Institute, UC Berkeley

events.title: REI Colloquium: Sanctuary Making: Immigrant Families Reshaping Geographies of Deportability
events.location: Social Sciences Building 402 Barrows Hall Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Sanctuary Making: Immigrant Families Reshaping Geographies of Deportability Imigration policy and enforcement practices in the United States now extend beyond the border to the country's interior, impacting the private lives of millions of undocumented and mixed-status families in new ways. Sanctuary Making traces this shift, showing how as enforcement has expanded and deepened, new "hot spots" have appeared across nontraditional sites such as neighborhoods, roads, worksites, hospitals, grocery stores, and homes. Undercurrents of fear, anxiety, and loss permeate the everyday lives of the families navigating these terrains of enforcement. Carolina Valdivia reveals the emotional and material labor of young adults that often underpins families' sanctuary making efforts—strategies to shield against the worst outcomes of enforcement. Many young adults are compelled to take on parental responsibilities and serve as a primary source of emotional support for family members while also brokering legal processes tied to their family's immigration cases. How might policymakers, organizers, educators, and the wider community better support these young people in their efforts to create sanctuary for their families in an increasingly hostile landscape? More about the book: https://www.ucpress.edu/books/sanctuary-making/paper (https://www.ucpress.edu/books/sanctuary-making/paper)This event is co-sponsored by the UC Berkeley Center for Race and Gender and the Berkeley Interdisciplinary Migration Initiative.About the Speaker:Carolina Valdivia is an Associate Professor of Criminology, Law and Society at the University of California, Irvine. Carolina's research interests include immigration, law and society, the sociology of education, race and ethnicity, youth and families, and the U.S.-Mexico borderlands. Her work explores how various forms of legal and social exclusion impact the lives of immigrant youth and their families, including their educational trajectories, mental health, and political participation. You can find the rest of her biography here: https://carolinavaldivia.org/ (https://carolinavaldivia.org/)This is an accessible event. events.title: What Can Israeli Theatre Do? From Screen to Stage with Ronnie Brodetzky
events.description: Helen Diller Institute Literary Series, Session I*Co-sponsored by the Center for Jewish Studies and the Department of Comparative Literature, UC BerkeleyPublic Event What can Israeli theatre say at a moment when the boundaries of permissible speech are being fiercely contested? Ronnie Brodetzky, one of Israel's most successful contemporary theatre directors, belongs to a new generation of women reshaping a field long dominated by men. From bold stagings of canonical works such as Tartuffe and Twelfth Night to experimental productions like Typing…, created from real WhatsApp conversations, and How to Get Up from a Chair, inspired by YouTube tutorials, Brodetzky transforms both dramatic literature and the media of everyday life into surprising theatrical forms. In conversation with Yael Segalovitz, she will discuss making art amid Israel's political pressures, turning private speech into public performance, and what live theatre can reveal about contemporary Israeli society. Expect a lively conversation about art, politics, digital life, and the pleasures and perils of putting Israel onstage.Ronnie Brodetzky, Israeli theatre director, creator, and writer; winner of the 2020 Rosenblum Performing Arts Award and 2023 Directing Award by The Cameri Theatre; author of An Almost Olympic-Sized Pool (2016)Yael Segalovitz, Joan Bieder Visiting Professor of Jewish and Hebrew Literature, Helen Diller Institute, UC Berkeley; Comparative Literature Department, UC Berkeley; Assistant Professor, Ben-Gurion University of the NegevRegister: https://HDILiterarySeries2.rsvpify.com (https://HDILiterarySeries2.rsvpify.com)

events.title: Geography Colloquia Series - Teacher Organizing Across the Americas: Diverse Strategies for Transforming Unions, Schools, and Society
events.description: Teacher Organizing Across the Americas explores why teachers' unions in Brazil, Mexico, and the United States, representing similar constituencies and fighting for comparable goals, have embraced radically different strategies. Through an ethnographic comparison of teacher organizing in São Paulo, Oaxaca, and New York, the book focuses on three key strategies in teacher organizing—leftist party politics, autonomist politics, and interest group politics—to demonstrate how the strategic choices teachers make matter for both schools and society. In São Paulo, teachers' leftist party politics helped to elect pro-labor presidents five times, with significant social reforms; yet these same politics failed to influence education policy and led to factionalism within the union. In Oaxaca, teachers' autonomous politics led to robust cultural initiatives, an innovative pedagogical proposal, and the capacity to boycott national education reforms. Finally, in many U.S. cities in the 2000s, teachers rejected interest group politics in favor of rank-and-file caucuses that prioritized union-community coalitions and racial justice, which also created new fault lines within the unions and an ambiguous relationship with electoral politics. Teaching Organizing Across the Americas offers important lessons for both scholars and activists interested in transforming institutions like unions to promote more just schools and societies. Rebecca Tarlau is Associate Professor of Education at Stanford University and former Associate Professor of Labor and Employment Relations at Pennsylvania State University, where she was the co-founder of the Consortium for Social Movements and Education Research and Practice. Her ethnographic research focuses on theories of the state and state-society relations; social movements and popular education; Latin American education and development; and labor movements and teachers' work. She is the author of the award-winning Occupying School, Occupying Land: How the Landless Workers Movement Transformed Brazilian Education (OUP, 2019).

events.title: EECS Colloquium: Quantum Interconnects and Modularity via Waveguide QED
events.description: In this talk, we present a demonstration of entanglement distribution via directional photon emission and absorption along a microwave waveguide [1,2]. Superconducting qubits couple to the waveguide at multiple, well-separated locations through modules that deterministically emit and absorb single microwave photons. Using this architecture, we demonstrate directional single-photon emission with 96% fidelity and single-photon absorption exceeding 60% efficiency. We then use partial emission and absorption to generate remote entanglement – a four-qubit W-state ��� between qubits in the emitter and absorber modules with 62% fidelity. Time permitting, we also present an example of driven dissipative entanglement reaching 89% fidelity [3]. These works along with 3D integration target modular and extensible quantum information processing mediated by quantum interconnects. [1] B. Kannan, et al., Nature Physics 19, 394 (2023) | arXiv:2203.01430 (2022) [2] A. Almanakly, et al., Nature Physics 21, 825 (2025) | arXiv:2408.05164 (2024) [3] A. Almanakly, et al., arXiv:2606.13375 (2026) William D. Oliver is jointly appointed the Henry Ellis Warren (1894) Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and Professor of Physics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where he leads the Engineering Quantum Systems Group. He is presently on partial leave as Chief Engineer withGoogle Quantum AI. Will's research interests include the materials growth, fabrication, design, control, and measurement of superconducting qubit processors. From 2003-2023, Will also worked at MIT Lincoln Laboratory – most recently as Laboratory Fellow (2017-2023) – where he was instrumental in growing the quantum computing group to its present levels. Will stepped down from this position to co-found Atlantic Quantum, a quantum computing start-up. Atlantic Quantum was acquired by Google in October 2025. Will is elected Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, Fellow of the American Physical Society, and Fellow of the IEEE. He also serves on the U.S. National Quantum Initiative Advisory Committee. Will earned his Ph.D. in Electrical Engineering from Stanford University, his M.S. in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science from MIT, and a B.S. in Electrical Engineering and B.A. in Japanese from the University of Rochester (NY).

events.title: ERG Colloquium Series Fall 2026: Marshall Burke
events.description: Description: Wildfires and the smoke they produce are the fastest growing environmental threat in the US and many other parts of the world. I review recent advances in the measurement of smoke and its constituents, and recent advances in the quantification of both short- and long-term health impacts from smoke exposure and from exposure to the fires themselves. We estimate that short-run smoke exposure causes tens of thousands of deaths annually, a number that will likely grow due to climate change absent substantial intervention. We study the impacts of a leading proposed intervention – prescribed burning – and estimate meaningful net reductions in smoke exposure if the state were to meet its stated prescribed burning targets. Bio: Marshall Burke is professor of Global Environmental Policy in the Doerr School of Sustainability at Stanford, and a senior fellow at the Stanford Woods Institute for the Environment, Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies, and Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, all at Stanford. He is also a research fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research. He holds a PhD in Agricultural and Resource Economics from UC Berkeley, and a BA in International Relations from Stanford. He directs the Environmental Change and Human Outcomes Lab at Stanford, is co-founder of AtlasAI, and co-creator of the Environmental Hazards Adaptation Atlas.

events.title: Expecting Inequity: How the Maternal Health Crisis Affects Even the Wealthiest Black Americans
events.description: Racism in maternal healthcare is not reserved for the poor. Wealthier black people are much more likely to die during pregnancy, childbirth, or the postpartum period than their white counterparts. Expecting Inequityfocuses on a San Francisco obstetrics clinic that caters to the affluent, examining the choices around prenatal care and childbirth that class-privileged, pregnant black people are making in order to survive what has been called the "black maternal health crisis."Khiara M. Bridges is the Earl Warren Professor of Public Law at UC Berkeley School of Law. She is a nationally-recognized expert on the intersection of race, class, and reproductive rights. Her scholarship has appeared in the most influential law reviews in the country, including the flagship law journals at Harvard, Yale, Stanford, and UC Berkeley, among many others. She is also the author of several books: Reproducing Race: An Ethnography of Pregnancy as a Site of Racialization (2011), The Poverty of Privacy Rights (2017), and Critical Race Theory: A Primer (2019, 2026). Her fourth book, Expecting Inequity: How the Maternal Health Crisis Affects Even the Wealthiest Black Americans, was released in March 2026. Bridges graduated as valedictorian from Spelman College, receiving her degree in three years. She received her J.D. from Columbia Law School and her Ph.D., with distinction, from Columbia University's Department of Anthropology. She speaks fluent Spanish and basic Arabic, and she is a classically-trained ballet dancer who danced professionally in New York City for twenty years before moving to the Bay Area.

events.title: From Evening Fog to Light and Dark: What Sōseki took from "The Tale of Genji"
events.description: Natsume Sōseki is usually read as the Japanese novelist who learned his craft from the West. But what did he take from Murasaki Shikibu, his greatest Japanese predecessor? Although he claimed not to care much for the Tale of Genji, I present evidence in the talk that Sōseki did read the Genji closely. Tracing echoes of the Genji in Sanshiro,The Gate, Kokoro, and Light and Dark, I argue that Sōseki learned more from Lady Muraski than he acknowledged about how the art of the novel can shed light on the darkest corners of the emotional lives of men and women. [BIO] Keith Vincent teaches in the Department of World Languages & Literatures at Boston University, where he directs the MFA Program in Literary Translation. Recent publications include "Genji's Ghosts" in The Literary Imagination (Spring 2026) and "Proust in Japan and Japan in Proust: Notes on Yoshida Jō and the École japonaise of Proust Studies" in Global Japanese History and Culture(Routledge, 2026). Forthcoming this year is an essay on Proust and TheThousand and One Nights.

events.title: [BCLB] Smaller Scope, High Stakes: The EU Due Diligence Directive and Business
events.organizer: Berkeley Center for Law and Business
events.description: The EU’s Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) was once billed as the most ambitious corporate accountability law in the world. It creates a direct obligation on corporations to conduct sustainability and human rights due diligence. Then came the Omnibus. The scope has narrowed and the timeline has shifted, but the directive has not gone away, and it still reaches large non-EU companies with significant business in the EU. What does the CSDDD now require, which U.S. companies remain in scope, and what cannot be negotiated away? Looking ahead, how might further changes to EU rules and diverging U.S. approaches reshape companies’ obligations and strategies, and what should businesses be doing now? This BCLB webinar brings together academic, advisory, and law firm perspectives on what the directive means in practice: why it matters for business, how companies are approaching implementation, and whether it makes a real difference for the workers and communities it is meant to protect. Confirmed Speakers: Gustavo Becker, Executive Research Fellow, Berkeley Center for Law and Business Faris Natour, Principal and Co-Founder, Article One Ashley Walter, Partner and Chief Sustainability Officer, Orrick Moderator: Sanchita Banerjee Saxena, Professional faculty member, Haas School of Business and Senior Academic Fellow, Berkeley Center for Law and Business Register here

events.title: Alessandro Ori: From Translation Stalling to Organellar Maps: Molecular Drivers and Therapeutic Targets in Brain Aging and Neurodegeneration
events.description: Aging is the primary risk factor for major neurodegenerative disorders, driven by a progressive breakdown of cellular proteostasis. Yet, uncovering the precise causal mechanisms—and translating them into viable therapeutic strategies—remains a fundamental challenge. In this seminar, I will discuss multi-omics and proteomic advances that illuminate disease drivers across scales, from protein synthesis defects to organellar dysfunction. First, using the turquoise killifish brain aging model, we reveal that protein-transcript decoupling is fueled by ribosome pausing and disome accumulation at basic amino acid stretches (Arg, Lys). This stalling stems from altered tRNA charging, declining building block availability, and molecular ribosome aging, leading to the selective loss of critical RNA-binding proteins like TDP-43. Second, applying cell-type-specific LysoTag proteomics across intact mouse brain lineages, we established a brain lysosome atlas that uncovered cell-tailored organellar functions and novel disease-relevant proteins, notably the neuron-specific glucose transporter SLC45A1 whose loss compromises lysosomal pH and mitochondrial integrity. Furthermore, comparative profiling across neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis models identified a shared lysosomal disease signature centering on sphingolipid catabolism and organelle contact sites. Finally, I will highlight how high-throughput perturb-proteomics in human iPSC-derived neurons couples arrayed CRISPR screening with global proteomic readouts to map TDP-43 loss-of-function phenotypes and accelerate therapeutic target discovery.Division(s): MTx (Molecular Therapeutics)

events.title: The maintenance of diversity in plant communities: insights from Amazonian forest dynamics and California serptentine annual plants
events.description: Despite centuries of research, many fundamental features of the structure and dynamics of plant communities defy simple explanation. My research group pursues general answers to these questions through integrative approaches that combine community ecology perspectives with insights from functional ecology, floristics and macroecology. Our lab uses a variety of observational, theoretical and experimental approaches, many of them rooted in plant collections and functional trait databases. First, I will share recent projects exploring the dynamics of a large forest plot in the hyperdiverse Ecuadorian Amazon, where we use functional-trait based approaches and novel computational tools to explore the ways in which edaphic specialization, spatial aggregation, and competition dynamics shape one of the most species-rich forests on the planet. Next, I will highlight our recent work in annual plant communities associated with serpentine soils in coastal California, a species-rich system that is ideal for detailed, theoretically-grounded experiments to disentangle mechanisms of species coexistence. Our recent experimental work demonstrates how species trait differences, contrasting responses to spatial and temporal environmental heterogeneity, and complex higher-order interactions combine to shape the diversity of these systems at both local and landscape scales. Finally, I will share insights from my lab's work on continental and global scale patterns of plant diversity, work that is intimately connected to the development of plant trait and occurrence databases. Taken together, these efforts inform our understanding of the mechanisms that drive the fundamental distribution of plant diversity and function across the planet, as well as our predictions of how species and communities will respond to ongoing global change.

events.title: Hitchcock Grant Lecture with Kelly Lytle Hernández | Racist by Design - Two Centuries of U.S. Immigration Control
events.location: Banatao Auditorium, Sutardja Dai Hall - UC Berkeley Campus
events.description: In this lecture, award winning historian Kelly Lytle Hernández will be presenting her work, Racist by Design. She reveals how generations of lawmakers and law enforcers built the American immigration system to encourage white immigrants while targeting nonwhite migrants for exclusion, punishment, and removal. The goal, often explicitly stated by the system's architects, was to create a permanent caste of undocumented and criminalized workers to provide cheap labor for the American economy.About Kelly Lytle Hernández Professor Kelly Lytle Hernández holds The Thomas E. Lifka Endowed Chair in History at UCLA. Her major publications are Migra! A History of the U.S. Border Patrol (University of California Press, 2010), City of Inmates: Conquest, Rebellion, and the Rise of Human Caging in Los Angeles (University of North Carolina Press, 2017), and Bad Mexicans: Race, Empire, and Revolution in the Borderlands (W. W. Norton, 2022). Her forthcoming book, Racist by Design: Two Centuries of U.S. Immigration Control, will be published by W. W. Norton in 2026. In 2016, Professor Lytle Hernández established Million Dollar Hoods (MDH), a university-based but community-driven research initiative that maps the fiscal and human costs of mass incarceration in Los Angeles. She served as the MDH director until 2024 and now serves as the initiative's principal advisor. Professor Lytle Hernández is currently a principal investigator for two additional research collaborations: Mapping Deportations, which maps the history of mass deportation from the United States, and Archiving the Age of Mass Incarceration, which preserves a historic cache of LAPD files and documents the impact of policing on LA residents since the 1970s. For her historical and contemporary work, Professor Lytle Hernández's scholarship has been awarded numerous prizes and honors, including a MacArthur "Genius" Fellowship, and she is currently an elected member of the Society of American Historians, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and the Pulitzer Prize Board.

events.title: Matrix on Point: Propaganda Machines
events.description: REGISTER In the age of AI, what is the future of "public truths"? AI-driven tech platforms and companies, influencers, and deepfakes are issuing ever-new challenges for journalism, media integrity, and related mechanisms through which democratic societies hold power to account. At the same time, universities – erstwhile guardians of critical inquiry and independent knowledge production – are increasingly entering into partnerships with AI companies, in a new kind of knowledge compact. This panel brings together scholars of AI and influence in journalism, media, and California's universities to address this technology's increasingly powerful role in the current U.S. landscape of information and knowledge politics. The panel will feature Maty Bohacek, Researcher at Stanford University; Martha Kenney, Professor of Women & Gender Studies at San Francisco State University; Martha Lincoln, Associate Professor of Anthropology at SF State; and Edward Wasserman, Professor of Journalism at UC Berkeley. Cori Hayden, Director of Social Science Matrix and Robert H. Lowie Professor of Anthropology, will moderate. This event is co-sponsored by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies (IGS), the Berkeley Economy and Society Initiative (BESI), the UC Berkeley School of Information, and the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences (EECS).PanelistsMaty Bohacek (https://matybohacek.com/) is a researcher at Stanford University, working at the intersection of AI and media integrity. In a world that is becoming increasingly AI-mediated, his goal is to build AI systems and networks that are inherently trustworthy and interpretable, resulting in productive, democratic discourse. Maty built a deepfake detector for President Zelenskyy of Ukraine and created a deepfake CNN news anchor, which opened a primetime news segment to raise awareness of AI threats. Beyond media integrity, he demonstrated that AI models trained on their own data collapse, developed a method to determine whether specific data were used to train a model, and developed an AI-powered sign language translator. His work has been featured in Forbes, CNN, Science, Nature, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, and others.Martha Kenney (https://transforms.sfsu.edu/martha-kenney) is a Professor of Women & Gender Studies at San Francisco State University. She earned a Ph.D. from the History of Consciousness at UC Santa Cruz, where she was a founding member of the Science & Justice Research Center. Located in the tradition of feminist science studies, her research examines how narratives from new fields of biomedical research — such as environmental epigenetics and precision medicine—support, contest, and reconfigure collective visions of social justice, environmental justice, and health equity. She has a track record of collaborative, interdisciplinary inquiry, often publishing with colleagues across institutions and national contexts. She was recently a TUM Global Visiting Professor at the Department of Science, Technology, and Society at the Technical University of Munich. She is currently a Health Equity Institute Faculty Scholar at SFSU.Martha Lincoln (https://anthropology.sfsu.edu/people/martha-lincoln) is a medical and cultural anthropologist. Prior to joining the Anthropology Department at SF State in 2017, she received her Ph.D. from the Graduate Center of the City University of New York and completed a postdoctoral fellowship at the Prevention Research Center, affiliated with UC Berkeley's School of Public Health. Broadly, her research addresses the cultural politics of public health, biopolitics, and the effects of political economic change on health systems and health outcomes. Since 2008, she has conducted field research in Vietnam, leading to published research on Hanoi's informal sector, stratification and deregulation in health care provision, the ghosts of war, alcohol use and drinking cultures, the redefinition of poverty under late socialism, and urban cholera outbreaks. Her book, Epidemic Politics in Contemporary Vietnam: Public Health and the State, was published in 2021 by Bloomsbury Academic. She serves as co-editor-in-chief of the Journal of Vietnamese Studies. Her current project is based in the United States, and focuses on affective economies in medical crowdfunding for cancer.Edward Wasserman (https://journalism.berkeley.edu/person/ed_wasserman/), Professor of Journalism at UC Berkeley, served as Dean of the Graduate School of Journalism from 2013 to 2020. Before coming to Berkeley, he spent a decade as the John S. and James L. Knight Foundation Professor of Journalism Ethics at Washington and Lee University, home of the nation's first college-level journalism program. Wasserman's journalism career spanned 30 years. He was CEO and editor in chief of American Lawyer Media's Miami-based Daily Business Review newspaper chain, executive business editor of The Miami Herald, city editor of The Casper (Wyo.) Star-Tribune, and editorial director of Primedia's 140-publication Media Central division in New York. Wasserman received a B.A. cum laude in politics and economics from Yale, a licence in philosophy from the University of Paris I, and a Ph.D. from the London School of Economics, where his thesis was on the politics of innovation in communications technology.Cori Hayden (https://anthropology.berkeley.edu/cori-hayden)'s research and teaching focus on the anthropology of science, technology, and medicine. She received her PhD in Anthropology from UC Santa Cruz in 2000 and has held fellowships at the Center for US-Mexican Studies in San Diego, the University of Cambridge, and the Center for Advanced Studies in the Social and Behavioral Sciences (CASBS) in Palo Alto. At Berkeley, she has served as the Chair of the Department of Anthropology and was the Director of the Center for Science, Technology, Medicine, and Society from 2010-2013. Hayden is the author of When Nature Goes Public: The Making and Unmaking of Bioprospecting in Mexico (Princeton University Press, 2003), and The Spectacular Generic: Pharmaceuticals and the Simipolitical in Mexico (2023, Duke University Press). Her more recent research and writing projects explore, respectively, the reanimation of crowd theory as an avenue for exploring contemporary market formations, political atmospheres, and modes of inquiry; and the sciences of Long Covid in a moment of resurgent authoritarianisms.

events.title: Fascism After Work: Post-Fordism, Abandonment, and Care
events.description: This work-in-progress seminar asks what fascism looks like after the eclipse of the factory as capitalism's organizing stage of exploitation. Delivered in the run-up to the 2026 midterm elections and near the first anniversary of Paolo Virno's death, the seminar returns to Virno's account of post-Fordism to track how immaterial labor—the shared linguistic, cognitive, and affective capacity Virno saw as a site of potential liberation—has become the privileged site of extraction and, for many, of organized abandonment. Bringing Virno into dialogue with Black studies (Ruth Wilson Gilmore especially), the seminar argues that today's political ambivalence—the same capacities that promise exodus also expose populations to premature death—demands a new diagnosis of fascism, one grounded not in discipline but in freedom, deregulation, and a disfigured abolitionism. As the midterms reopen the question of what kind of political order the United States is choosing, the seminar closes by asking what infrastructures of care and sociality might sustain good lives amidst labor's ruins.Lorenzo Fabbri is a McKnight Land-Grant Associate Professor of French and Italian at the University of Minnesota Twin Cities. Author of Cinema is the Strongest Weapon. Race-Making and Resistance in Fascist Italy (University of Minnesota Press, 2023).

events.title: Lia, Mira, Maria: Performance/Reading with Marília Garcia (2026 Brazilian Writer-in-Residence)
events.location: Spanish & Portuguese Library, 5125 Dwinelle, Level E
events.description: What are the stages of mourning? Which path should one follow: that of memory? That of the archive (papers, traces)? After the loss of her mother, Lia, and of a friend, Maria, the author is eventually led to the monotypes of the Swiss-born artist Mira Schendel, who lived in Brazil. In the 1960s, Mira would sit in her kitchen and "engrave," in the presence of friends, drawings on the backs of Japanese paper, making lines and writing letters on the reverse side of the paper with a pointed object. Through this and other material and manual processes (handling papers, sorting through photographs, taking up swimming), the book Lia, Mira, Maria seeks to move through the stages of mourning. It includes images from archives, artworks, and family photographs, composing a kind of personal album of mourning. The performance combines the reading of a text with the live projection of images. The performance will be in English and will be followed by a conversation between Marília Garcia and Nathaniel Wolfson. Marília Garcia is a poet, translator, and researcher at the Rui Barbosa Foundation. She is the author of, among other books, Câmera lenta (Companhia das Letras, 2017; Oceanos Prize), Expedição: nebulosa (Companhia das Letras, 2023), and Pensar com as mãos (WMF Martins Fontes, 2025). In English, her chapbook The territory is not the map, translated by Hilary Kaplan, was published by Ugly Duckling Presse in 2017.

events.location: Magnes Collection of Jewish Art and Life, 2121 Allston Way, Berkeley, CA
events.description: Annual Diller Lecture Reception and Light Refreshments: 5:00-5:30pm Presentation and Conversation 5:30-7:00pm The 1948 Arab-Israeli War attracted attention from the highest levels of international society, state governments, transnational NGOs, journalism, and public opinion. Palestine and the emerging state of Israel functioned as both a mirror and a magnifier. Israel's establishment and the Palestinian Nakba were interpreted through countries' specific interests, histories, and cultures. These events also elicited tremendous passion. Palestine's mirroring and magnifying effects did not originate in 1948, but the events of that year drastically augmented them, and the patterns of global reaction remain with us to this day. To register for this event, please click this link. (https://forms.gle/e1v2ubg7fkEif56n8)Derek Penslar is the William Lee Frost Professor of Jewish History and the Director of the Center for Jewish Studies (https://cjs.fas.harvard.edu/) at Harvard University. Derek previously taught at Indiana University, the University of Toronto, and the University of Oxford, where he was the inaugural holder of the Stanley Lewis Chair in Modern Israel Studies. Derek has published a dozen books, including Theodor Herzl: The Charismatic Leader (2020) and Zionism: An EmotionalState (2023). He is currently writing a book titled The War for Palestine, 1947-1949: A Global History. events.title: One In A Million: film screening and Q&A
events.description: Join us for a screening of Frontline's new award-winning documentary One in a Million. Filmed over 10 years, it follows Israa's epic journey from Syria to Germany and back again. She and her family navigate war, exile, and heartbreak in a foreign land, revealing the complexities of the refugee experience. After the film, producer and Frontline Editor-In-Chief Raney Aronson-Rath will speak with Berkeley Journalism's Jason Spingarn-Koff and take questions. Snacks will be available before the screening in the lobby. RSVP HERE (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSeWjaO2EXvnExACSuCMOGInO8-TQ4f1rSaYPWarYbBSZu61cg/viewform?usp=publish-editor). In September 2015, filmmakers Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes met Israa, an 11-year-old Syrian girl selling cigarettes on a street corner in Turkey, alongside her father, Tarek. The family had fled Aleppo to join the largest movement of people since the Second World War. Together they trekked through Eastern Europe before finding refuge in Germany, where more than one million asylum seekers were registered by the end of that year. For ten years, the filmmakers continued to document Israa's life as the challenges of integration and cultural adjustment led to family breakdown as Western culture clashed with Syrian traditions. Following the fall of the Assad regime in 2025, the culminates when the filmmakers follow Israa, now a mother herself, back to the ruins of Aleppo as she confronts her own questions of identity and belonging. The film is a Sundance Winner for both the 'Audience Award: World Cinema Documentary' and the 'World Cinema Documentary Directing Award'.

events.title: Film Screening: The Secret
events.description: Loosely based on a real-life double-homicide case, Ann Hui's grisly debut feature is a key film of the early Hong Kong New Wave. A young couple has been murdered—strung up in the woods—and Lin (Sylvia Chang), a friend of one of the victims, takes it upon herself to investigate. Interviews provide scarce clues, but every tree, alleyway, and red coat suggest something spectral. "The airy musical leitmotifs of Violet Lam Man-yee's ghostly score send shivers down the spine" (Faith Everard, Senses of Cinema). Through a series of labyrinthine flashbacks, a refracted truth is revealed.

events.title: BETR/EECS Solid State Technologies Seminar: Prof. Vivian Feig, Stanford University | Engineering Piezoelectric Biomaterials Across Length Scales for Transient Bioelectronics
events.description: Abstract: Bioelectronic technologies hold immense potential for monitoring, stimulating, and interfacing with living systems, but realizing their full impact requires materials that are less invasive, more adaptive, and accessible for widespread use. Achieving this vision demands new approaches that address the entire device lifecycle: from sustainable sourcing of raw materials; to integration with soft and dynamic tissues; to maintaining stable function over operational lifetimes; and ultimately to safe degradation or removal. Biomolecules are attractive building blocks for this task. Certain amino acids and peptides can assemble into crystalline structures that combine piezoelectricity with abundant, biodegradable, and chemically tunable components. But several challenges must be addressed before these molecules can be used to build practically useful materials. In this talk, I will discuss how my group engineers biomolecule-based piezoelectric materials across length scales to tune key performance attributes like stability and sensitivity to specific deformation modes. This work lays the foundation for new transient bioelectronic sensors and energy harvesters built from simple, naturally occurring molecules. Bio: Dr. Vivian Feig (pronounced "F-eye-g") is the Reid and Polly Anderson Faculty Fellow, Gabilan Fellow, and Assistant Professor of Mechanical Engineering and, by courtesy, Materials Science and Engineering at Stanford University. She has a multi-disciplinary background with academic and industrial training in chemical, materials, mechanical, and biomedical engineering. She obtained her B.S. in Chemical Engineering from Columbia University in 2012 and then spent 3 years working in the petrochemicals industry in both scale-up and manufacturing. In 2020, she obtained her PhD. in Materials Science and Engineering from Stanford University as a National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate (NDSEG) fellow under the guidance of Prof. Zhenan Bao. Subsequently, she received the Schmidt Science Fellows postdoctoral fellowship, which allowed her to pivot into translational medical research and mechanical engineering by joining the labs of Prof. Giovanni Traverso and Prof. Robert Langer at MIT and the Brigham and Women's Hospital.

events.title: Composition Colloquium: Julius Dobos
events.location: Morrison Hall Room 125, UC Berkeley Campus, 94720
events.description: TITLE:Spatial Composition: The New Frontier Composers have been using rhythm and melody for thousands of years; harmony for centuries. Musique concrète expanded the use of timbre some 75 years ago. Are we on the verge of another musical disruption? What if, using spatial location and movement as compositional tools, songwriters, composers, and producers not only mixed but composed in and for immersive systems? Can SPACE be considered a new element of music? Do spatial decisions made during the composition phase have an effect on the musical content itself? Do listeners respond differently to spatially composed music than to immersive mixes of non-spatial concepts? How should one approach writing in an immersive environment to yield conceptually novel musical content? Based on his latest research in spatial composition and reflecting the global interest among music professionals in its findings, this presentation and immersive demonstration by composer Julius Dobos explores the use of spatial location and movement in music composition and production.

events.title: "The Smallest Unit of Liberation": Kuleana, Community, & Movement Building with Dr. Jamaica Heolimeleikalani Osorio
events.description: Register here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSck0HiXajzxnYA-1toomi9Q11AQkUjSVXio5GojYDxBJDbh-g/viewform?usp=dialog). Please note that space is limited. Confirmation information will be shared upon registration and as capacity allows."The Smallest Unit of Liberation": Kuleana, Community, and Movement Building This two-part workshop explores how we build movements rooted in deep relationships, collective responsibility, and intentional strategy. Grounded in the premise articulated by @eroticsofliberation that "relationships are the smallest unit of liberation," we begin by strengthening our understanding of kuleana—our responsibilities to one another, our communities, and the lands that sustain us. We then turn to the practical work of developing campaigns, sharpening our organizing strategies, and building the collective power necessary to win. Because liberation is not something we achieve alone, we must learn not only how to fight together, but how to build the relationships and movements that can sustain that fight.Part One: How Does Your Kuleana Move You? In this hands-on writing workshop, we will use poetry and storytelling to explore the many layers of kuleana, including our responsibilities to ourselves, our families, our lands, and our communities, as well as the privileges and obligations that shape how we show up in movement work. Through guided writing exercises, we will map our relationships, reflect on how we care for what we hold dear, and practice bringing those commitments to life through storytelling. No prior writing experience is necessary—just a willingness to reflect, imagine, and create. Participants will leave with a deeper understanding of the kuleana that shapes who we are, how we relate to one another, and how we move in the world.Part Two: Kiaʻi Basics—Campaigns, Strategy, and the Work of Getting Free Made possible through the movement training and organizing experience of SOUL, RUKUS Society, and the Huli Movement, this truncated facilitated learning workshop gets into the nitty-gritty of building effective campaigns and movements. We will explore the relationships between strategy, tactics, targets, messaging, and security culture, asking how these elements work together to build power and advance our collective struggles. Through discussion and practical exercises, we will examine not only what it takes to organize a campaign, but how to make strategic decisions, respond to challenges, and build movements capable of sustaining themselves over time.Dr. Jamaica Heolimeleikalani Osorio is a Kanaka Maoli organizer, artist, scholar, and public intellectual whose work is rooted in aloha ʻāina and the struggle for collective liberation. Born and raised in Hawaiʻi, Jamaica is a longtime participant in movements for Kanaka ʻŌiwi sovereignty, land and water protection, demilitarization, decolonization, and is the Vice President the Hawaiian National organization of Hui Aloha ʻĀina o Honolulu. Her organizing, teaching, and creative work are grounded in a belief that movements are sites of knowledge-making and that another world is not only possible, but already being built through collective action. Jamaica is also an Associate Professor of Indigenous and Native Hawaiian Politics at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, where she teaches and writes at the intersections of Indigenous sovereignty, abolition, militarism, and collective liberation. Her work moves across the boundaries of scholarship, poetry, film, and movement organizing. She is the author of the award-winning Remembering Our Intimacies: Moʻolelo, Aloha ʻĀina, and Ea (https://www.nativebookshawaii.org/products/remembering-our-intimacies) (University of Minnesota Press, 2021) and her poetry and activism are the subject of the award-winning film This Is the Way We Rise (Sundance 2021). She was also a lead artist and co-writer of the award winning VR documentary On the Morning You Wake (To the End of the World) (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KyTb_56XzN8) (Premier:Sundance 2022 and XR Experience Jury Award at SXSW). Across these forms, Jamaica's work asks what it means to build liberatory futures from the places, relationships, and movements that have survived colonial violence. She writes and organizes toward a world grounded in aloha ʻāina, collective responsibility, Indigenous sovereignty, abolition, and abundance—and toward movements powerful enough to make that world real.

events.title: Fizzah Sajjad | Speculation and Circulation: Real Estate Development and the Market for Land in Urban Pakistan
events.description: The S. S. Pirzada Lecture on Pakistan by Fizzah Sajjad (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6784), the winner of the S. S. Pirzada Dissertation Prize for 2025 for her dissertation titled, Speculation and Circulation: Real Estate Development and the Market for Land in Urban Pakistan (London School of Economics and Political Science, 2025).Sai Balakrishnan (https://ced.berkeley.edu/people/sai-balakrishnan), Associate Professor of City & Regional Planning, will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Fri, Nov 6, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————– ABSTRACT: This dissertation studies the dynamics of Lahore's rapidly expanding residential real estate market as a means to contextualize and understand growing housing pressures in the city. Specifically, it examines developer motivations and mechanisms of profitmaking to uncover why and how expansion has taken place in recent years, and in whose interests. By studying and centring the actions of supply side actors such as real estate developers, whose activities and modes of profitmaking remain understudied and undertheorized within existing scholarship, it investigates why the city's real estate market remains inaccessible for a majority of the city's residents. Drawing on sixteen months of fieldwork, this dissertation shows that actors in the business of land development in Lahore have devised a mechanism that overcomes constraints in accessing institutional finance and allows them to profit off land conversions without using their own resources. This mechanism – what I characterize as accumulation by speculative circulation – relies on market-making techniques and the circulation of a market-based instrument of land acquisition and sales known as 'the file' to finance land conversions. The file, as I show, is an object but also a future. It is a fictional commodity that turns 'land' into 'liquid' form, helping create a real estate market that is structured, first and foremost, to accommodate the interests of investors and state actors, rather than those looking to meet their housing needs. This thesis argues that the valorisation and repurposing of land for investment purposes serves as both site and mechanism of housing exclusion, contributing to spatial inequality in the city and heightening the odds against more equitable interventions. It also shows how state entities themselves are implicated in this accumulation model, and remain invested in furthering sprawl, gentrification and dispossession. By illustrating how speculative practices operate in real estate markets, especially in contexts where theory expects otherwise, the thesis contributes empirically and theoretically to questions of land commodification and peri-urban transformations, particularly in rapidly urbanizing cities of the Global South. It also extends and complicates theories of speculative urbanisms, financialization and dispossession. SPEAKER BIOFizzah Sajjad i (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6784)s an Assistant Professor at the Lahore University of Management Sciences. Her research focuses on questions of land, housing, transport and the politics of infrastructure development in rapidly urbanizing cities of the Global South. Fizzah holds a PhD in Human Geography and Urban Studies from the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE) where her dissertation looked at speculative practices in residential real estate and the market for land in Lahore, Pakistan. She also has a Masters in City Planning from MIT.Her work has been published in leading journals including Antipode and Environment & Planning D, and she has co-edited the volume "Lahore in Motion: Infrastructure, History and Belonging in Urban Pakistan" (UCL Press, 2025). Fizzah also contributes to public scholarship through media outlets such as Dawn, Himal South Asia, and Jamhoor. Most recently, she was Co-Investigator on the project 'Navigating the grid in the 'world-class city: poverty, gender and access to services in India, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka,' under the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) GCRF '(Re)Thinking the Off-Grid City' programme. This work examined how the urban poor access basic services in South Asian cities. The Pakistan sub-project more specifically explored peri-urban expansion in the city of Lahore, focusing on transformations and service provision challenges in formerly rural 'urban villages' that are now surrounded and encircled by suburban residential real estate projects. events.title: Film Screening: Harakiri
events.description: Masaki Kobayashi harnesses the breathtaking beauty of black-and-white, widescreen cinematography to create an abstract epic. Starring Tatsuya Nakadai, the film depicts one man's desperate attempt to crack the blind, absolute authority that characterizes the feudal age and, Kobayashi suggests, our own. In an Edo-period mansion, the camera inches down hallways and finds rooms within rooms to explicate a complex flashback narration. In the bloody climax, the black-robed figures who were caught and dissected by a stationary camera throughout the film come into their own as an inexorable prophecy, like Toru Takemitsu's haunting music and the words that emerge almost rhythmically from the dialogue: harakiri . . . (seppuku).

Strand A: Building Lessons for Real World Competence Collaborate, Innovate, Invigorate: Next-level Lessons for every classroom. Invigorate your teaching this year! You will collaborate to develop lessons that focus on teaching in the target language with comprehensible input, guided practice, grammar in context and formative assessment for all levels of proficiency. events.title: Film Screening: Kwaidan
events.description: Breathtakingly photographed on hand-painted sets, Kwaidan is at once a Japanese woodcut writ large, and an abstract wash of luminescent colors that seem to come from another world. An electronic soundtrack by avant-garde composer Toru Takemitsu plays hauntingly with natural sounds—crickets, rain, the cracking of wood, the loud silence of snow. Yet the stories—four of Lafcadio Hearn's ghostly tales—strangely contradict this plastic splendor in their simple, aching humanity. All are tales of mortals caught by forces beyond their comprehension when the supernatural world intervenes in their lives. This version of Kwaidan is the original three-hour Director's Cut.

events.title: Film Screening: The Human Condition I: No Greater Love
events.description: It is rare when an episode of national history can be interpreted without the burden of illusions, both obsolete and nostalgic. This is one of the great strengths of Masaki Kobayashi's The Human Condition, a nine-hour epic about Japan's occupation of China during World War II. The trilogy begins with an attack on inhuman practices in the Japanese army and ends with a bitter denunciation of Stalinism by the would-be-socialist hero, Kaji (the great Tatsuya Nakadai), a Japanese soldier who has confronted the reality of war and found it unyielding. In grand Dostoyevskian flourishes, Kobayashi suggests the impossibility of an individual altering the ethical standards of a social system. Standing in for the director, Kaji says, "Minor facts ignored by history can be fatal to the individual." It is Kobayashi's recognition of "minor facts" that joins the poetic to the journalistic in a scathing epic about the cruelties of war. This first part of the trilogy finds Kaji working as a supervisor in a forced labor camp in southern Manchuria, where he and his wife attempt to better the lot of the enslaved Chinese workers. Kaji is accused of dissent, tortured, and then inducted into the army.

Kobayashi’s monumental film can clarify and enrich your understanding of what it is to be alive” (New York Times).

events.title: Film Screening: Contempt
events.description: In Italy, Fritz Lang is shooting The Odyssey for an American producer (Jack Palance). Fritz mourns classical culture but will settle for swords and sandals; like The Odyssey, Contempt is about man against circumstances, and such is the circumstance of cinema. The screenwriter, Paul (Michel Piccoli), meanwhile, becomes lost in Rome, and during his odyssey, his wife, Camille (Brigitte Bardot), enters into a crisis of contempt. Contempt becomes very much Camille/Penelope's story as, on Paul's return, their marriage is dissected. With its colors and compositions, its ruins, its vistas, and especially its movement, Contempt is epic, but it is an epic stripped bare by its director.

events.description: Advantages in Korea’s Foreign Relations: A Constitutional and Institutional Perspective Korea has emerged as a key player on the global stage. Its journey through the 20th century was marked by colonization, war, extreme poverty and authoritarian regimes. Mr. Na Sang-deok, Deputy Consul General of Korea in San Francisco, draws on more than 20 years of experience as a Korean diplomat to highlight the distinctive characteristics, values, and historical experiences that have contributed to modern Korea and its diplomacy. Cho Chair, Center for Korean Studies, UC Berkeley). * Doors open from 11:30, with lunch reception and networking. * Event begins at 12:00. Registration is required. events.title: Condensed Matter Seminar with Harold Hwang: Superconductivity in layered nickelates
events.description: Superconductivity in layered nickelates Unconventional superconductivity in proximity to various strongly correlated phases has been a recurring theme in materials as diverse as heavy fermion compounds, cuprates, pnictides, and twisted bilayer graphene. Here we will discuss a growing family of layered nickelate superconductors. The initial discovery of superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelates was motivated by looking for an electronic analog of the cuprates. Notable aspects are a doping-dependent superconducting dome, strong magnetic fluctuations, and a landscape of unusual normal state properties from which superconductivity emerges. The subsequent discovery of superconductivity in bulk La3Ni2O7 under high pressure is quite intriguing, in that the d-electron configuration is a priori quite different. Recently, we have used epitaxial strain in (La,Pr)3Ni2O7 thin films to stabilize superconductivity at ambient pressure, which has enabled their extend experimental study and development.Bio: Harold Y. Hwang is the Shadi and Omid Farokhzad Professor in the School of Humanities and Sciences, of Applied Physics (Stanford University), of Photon Science (SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory), Senior Fellow of the Precourt Institute for Energy, and Director of the Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences. He received a BS in Physics, BS and MS in Electrical Engineering from MIT (1993), and a PhD in Physics from Princeton University (1997). He was formerly a Member of Technical Staff at Bell Laboratories (1996-2003) and on the faculty at the University of Tokyo (2003-2010). His research is in condensed matter and materials physics, with a focus on correlated electrons and emergent phenomena in quantum materials, and heterostructures for energy applications and devices. He is a fellow of the American Physical Society, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and member of the National Academy of Sciences. Recognitions include the MRS Outstanding Young Investigator Award (2005), the IBM Japan Science Prize (Physics, 2008), the Ho-Am Prize (Science, 2013), the Europhysics Prize (2014, with Jochen Mannhart and Jean-Marc Triscone), and the McGroddy Prize (2024).

events.title: Physics Colloquium with Wallace Marshall: Learning without a brain - how a single cell processes information
events.description: Learning without a brain - how a single cell processes information Abstract: Cells show a range of complex behaviors which might normally associated with cognition, including basic forms of learning such as habituation. The giant single-celled ciliate Stentor coeruleus is a pond-dwelling organism that attaches to substrates like pond plants and filter feeds by means of a ring of cilia at one end of the cell. Stentor cells can contract in response to mechanical stimulation, an effective escape mechanism but energetically costly. To avoid contracting due to random collision with non-threatening things like algae or pond plants, but still allow contraction when a large predator attacks, Stentor cells use a simple form of learning: when a cell is mechanically stimulated over and over again, it will gradually stop responding, representing a case of habituation. Our goal is to understand how a single cell learns, without a nervous system. We have developed automated devices for applying series of mechanical stimuli under computer control, which we are now using to test predictions of computational models for learning based on known or plausible biochemical mechanisms. Using this approach we have formulated a simplified biochemical model invoking known or suspected processes, which can account for all prior observations as well as new experiments designed to test the model. Based on this framework, we have investigated the molecular pathways involved in learning in Stentor, which suggests a role for CamKII kinase signaling in the learning process. Currently we are using a frequency domain analysis to probe the learning process, and find that the cell acts like a low pass filter with a fractional order transfer function, which provides us with a new way to discriminate among potential learning mechanisms. Biography: Wallace Marshall is Professor of Biochemistry and Biophysics at the University of California San Francisco. A native Long‐Islander, he received his bachelor's degrees in Electrical Engineering and Biochemistry from the State University of New York at Stony Brook, and his Ph.D. in Biochemistry from UC San Francisco, where he studied organization of chromosomes within the nucleus with John Sedat. He then moved to Yale University for postdoctoral studies with Joel Rosenbaum, where he became interested in questions of organelle size control and cell organization, using cilia, flagella, and centrioles as model systems. In 2003, he joined the faculty at UCSF where he continues to study questions of cellular organization in a variety of model organisms including green algae, yeast, ciliates, and mammalian cells. In recent years, his research program has expanded to include cellular engineering and the study of learning and computation in single cells. Dr. Marshall is an elected Fellow of the American Society for Cell Biology, former co‐director of the Physiology summer course at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole, Massachusetts, and he currently is Director of the Center for Cellular Construction, an NSF Science and Technology Center (STC) devoted to engineering cells and tissues.

events.title: The Bomb in/and/out of the Archive. feat. Zoé Samudzi
events.description: An Art, Technology, & Culture Colloquium lecture with Zoé Samudzi Postdoctoral scholar in the Department of African American and Africana Studies at Ohio State University - Monday, November 9, 2026 5:00 — 6:30 PM Eugene Jarvis Auditorium,Grimes Engineering Center (http://engineering.berkeley.edu/about/facilities/grimes-engineering-center/) RSVP here (https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSeykJAzTsXRPcjwOetCQvBjTYgUR_hNZbyFZzKTNKnwucsB-Q/viewform?usp=publish-editor)! Save the event to your bCal here (https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?action=TEMPLATE&tmeid=MHRhNmwwNmJwZGxrMGFvZjlkZ3M5MG1xc2IgZDV1NWVrN2o4aXBvZDBvOGlxNDE1ZTFhdnNAZw&tmsrc=d5u5ek7j8ipod0o8iq415e1avs%40group.calendar.google.com)! - Begun during her 2026 residency at La Becque in Switzerland, Zoé Samudzi presents the inaugural project of the research constellation "Can the African Steal?" Through archival photographs of the Belgian Congo (c. 1929-30) at Photo Elysée in Lausanne, Samudzi stitches together a variegated visual forensic through image absence through the deployment of the black planetary (after Canham and Seedat) as an onto-epistemic and transnational geographic frame. The negative spaces in the Swiss archive enable a positively articulated materiality of the atomic bomb. Her tracing of uranium extraction and/as warcraft conjoins King Leopold's free state and the Katangese mines in the Belgian Congo, the Trinity test in Los Alamos and Operation Crossroads in the Marshall Islands, and the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and nuclear afterlives in Japan. About Zoé Samudzi Zoé Samudzi is a postdoctoral scholar in the Department of African American and Africana Studies at The Ohio State University. She holds a PhD in Medical Sociology from the University of California, San Francisco. Her research contends with genocide memory and the multiplicity of denialisms, political mythologies of the postcolonial African state, visuality and the ethics of photographic seeing and witnessing, and the spatialities of racecraft and dispossession. An art critic and writer, Samudzi is an associate editor with Parapraxis Magazine, a popular magazine dedicated to psychoanalytic thinking. She is a 2026 Public Parking editorial resident, a 2026 Andy Warhol Foundation Arts Writers Grant grantee for her project, "The Citizen and the Anthropophage: Postwar/Postcolonial Italian Memory and the Cannibal Boom," a 2026 resident at La Becque's Principal Residency Program, and an awardee of the 2026 Fire Station Studios' International Curator Residency.
