events.title: Organic Chemistry Seminar
events.description: Marc Hillmyer, McKnight Presidential Endowed Chair, University of Minnesota Telechelic polymers for sustainable polyolefins Polyolefins are ubiquitous. They are lightweight, strong, and stable. These features render them useful in countless applications. Unfortunately, these attributes also contribute to the accumulation of persistent plastic waste in the environment. While polyolefins can be mechanically recycled, often this results in an inferior product and is in part the reason that only a small percentage of polyolefin products are effectively recycled. We have embarked on an effort to prepare polyolefins with functional groups at their chain ends. These telechelic polyolefins can be stitched together to form high molar mass plastics and thermosets. By virtue of the synthetic pathway used to make these materials, we generate products that include weak links along the backbones of the polymer chains. These links can be chemically cleaved to quantitatively deconstruct the material and allow for efficient chemical recycling back to the starting telechelic polymers that can be subsequently repolymerized. Our approach takes advantage of a tandem catalysis strategy that is perfectly atom economic and readily scalable. In this lecture I will discuss the preparation of the telechelic polyolefins and their use in the preparation of degradable polyolefin-based plastics and thermosets. I will also report on their materials properties, scalability, and recyclability.The Organic Seminar Series is sponsored by the William G. Dauben lecture fund

events.title: Ilyas Chattha | Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974
events.description: A talk by Ilyas Chattha (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6934), Associate Professor of History at the Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS), on his new book, Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974 (https://www.cambridge.org/us/universitypress/subjects/history/south-asian-history/citizens-traitors-bengali-internment-pakistan-19711974?format=HB&isbn=9781009568241) (Cambridge University Press, 2025). Drawing on previously untapped sources, the book examines Pakistan's internment of thousands of Bengalis after the 1971 war and explains why this history has largely been overlooked.Sadia Saeed (https://www.usfca.edu/faculty/sadia-saeed), Associate Professor of Sociology at the University of San Francisco will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies; Faculty Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies; Faculty Director, Global Studies and Global Poverty and Practice (https://blumcenter.berkeley.edu/academics/gppminor/), UC Berkeley. This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter). ————–DATE: Tue, November 10, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter) ————– ABOUT THE BOOKThe breakup of Pakistan in 1971—following a brutal civil war and military defeat by India—remains shrouded in layers of silence, myth, and contested memory. When the war ended, more than 90,000 Pakistani prisoners of war captured in East Pakistan, now Bangladesh, were transferred to Indian custody. In response, Pakistan interned a comparable number of Bengalis living in West Pakistan, treating them as leverage in negotiations for the prisoners' return. Neither group was allowed to go home immediately, creating what became one of the largest episodes of reciprocal mass internment since 1945. Drawing on a wide range of previously untapped sources, this book reconstructs the resulting crisis of captivity. It traces how Bengalis in West Pakistan were stripped of meaningful citizenship and recast as "traitors" and "enemies" in the aftermath of the Bangladesh War. More than half a century later, their internment remains largely absent from accounts of the most consequential political crisis in Pakistan's history. By recovering this neglected history, the book not only reveals the human and political consequences of mass detention but also explains how—and why—the experience of interned Bengalis was erased from the historical record. SPEAKER BIOIlyas Chattha (https://lums.edu.pk/lums_employee/6934) is Associate Professor of History at Lahore University of Management Sciences (LUMS) and a historian of modern South Asia. Educated at the universities of Warwick and Southampton in the United Kingdom, he has previously been affiliated with the Centre for Imperial and Post-Colonial Studies at the University of Southampton, the University of Warwick, and SOAS University of London. Dr Chattha's research focuses on late colonial Punjab, Partition, migration, borders and borderlands, collective violence, and the formation of the early postcolonial Pakistani state. He has written extensively on the long-term consequences of the partitions of 1947 and 1971, with particular attention to displacement, citizenship, internment, property, and state-building. He is the author of Citizens to Traitors: Bengali Internment in Pakistan, 1971–1974 (Cambridge University Press, 2025), which examines the wartime and postwar experiences of Bengalis interned in West Pakistan; The Punjab Borderland: Mobility, Materiality and Militancy, 1947–1987 (Cambridge University Press, 2022); and Partition and Locality: Violence, Migration and Development in Gujranwala and Sialkot, 1947–1961 (Oxford University Press, 2012). His current book project explores the history of evacuee and enemy property in Pakistan.EVENT POSTER _____________ Established in 2013 with a generous gift from the Subir & Malini Chowdhury Foundation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subir_Chowdhury), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (https://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/) at UC Berkeley champions the study of Bangladesh's cultures, peoples and history. The first of its kind in the US, the Center's mission is to create an innovative model combining research, scholarships, the promotion of art and culture, and the building of ties between institutions in Bangladesh and the University of California. Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/The-Subir-Malini-Chowdhury-Center-for-Bangladesh-Studies-752426458213022/?ref=hl) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952).PARKING INFORMATION (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/parking-around-campus)Please note that parking is not always easily available in Berkeley. events.title: Zoe Samudzi | Autotheorizing German Genocide Denial: A Dresden Museum Case Study
events.description: Following decades worth of efforts to broaden the historiographic and political boundaries of national genocide memory, German institutions have been pushed to contend with the country's history of colonial genocide, namely the attempted annihilation of Ovaherero and Nama people in the former colony of South West Africa (present-day Namibia). This lecture traces the contours of conflict that emerged from an invitation by the Staatlichen Kunstsammlungen Dresden (the Dresden State Art Collections) to produce an exhibition engaging the ethnopolitical threads of genocide denialism undergirding the relationship between East Germany and the South West Africa People's Organization (SWAPO) in relation to the history (and present afterlife) of the genocide. The institution's objection to a central claim that Germany had not fully recognized the Nama and Ovaherero genocide — one that reiterated existent tensions between the state's regime of memory as enforced by cultural institutions — compels consideration of how anti-black disciplining by a state institution might lead one to embrace withdrawal as an ethical imperative. Dr. Zoé Samudzi is a Provost's Fellow to Faculty scholar in the Department of African American and Africana Studies and an affiliated faculty in the Department of the History of Art. Her work contends with genocide memory and registers of denialism; political mythologies of the postcolonial African nation-state and the relationship between ethnicity and the national question; visuality and the ethics of photographic seeing; human remains and the state and community politics around repatriation and restitution; and the spatialities of racecraft and dispossession. She is a writer and critic, as well as an associate editor with Parapraxis Magazine; and she is 2026 Andy Warhol Foundation Arts Writers Grant grantee for her project, "The Citizen and the Anthropophage: Postwar/Postcolonial Italian Memory and the Cannibal Boom."If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) or information about campus mobility access features in order to fully participate in this event, please contact ies@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days before the event.

events.title: Under Pressure: Attitudes Towards China Among American Foreign Policy Professionals | Lecture by Rory Truex
events.description: How do social norms and professional incentives affect policy discourse within the Washington foreign policy community? We conducted over 50 semi-structured interviews and a survey of nearly five-hundred American foreign policy and national security professionals about their views towards the People's Republic of China. Over one fifth of survey respondents noted instances of professional pressure to voice a more hawkish point of view towards China, and many feared being perceived as naive or compromised by their views on, ties to, and experiences in China. These pressures were particularly acute for foreign policy professionals that are traditionally marginalized from power–those who are younger, non-white, or female. Our interview subjects reported a number of different coping strategies, including trying to communicate their views in the language of the perceived consensus. This "discourse mirroring" is distinct from preference falsification and self-censorship but may still contribute to difficulties in gauging peoples' true attitudes. Speaker BioRory Truex is Associate Professor of Politics and International Affairs at Princeton, where his research and teaching focuses on authoritarianism. He is the host of Civic Forum, a podcast about the big questions facing democracy, in the US and elsewhere.

events.title: The Narrowing Sea: Three Portraits of a Region

events.description: Speaker: Hannah Shepherd (Yale University) In Person Event | RSVP Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: This talk will introduce Hannah Shepherd's new book, The Narrowing Sea, via vignettes of the imperial region that developed across the Tsushima Straits between Pusan and Fukuoka in the seven decades from 1876 to 1953. It will offer the imperial region as a useful scale of analysis and connection between other imperial histories, and connect the urbanization of the imperial era with contemporary Japan's urban issues, before ending with a glimpse of new work that continues some of the histories and legacies discussed in The Narrowing Sea. Speaker Bio: Hannah Shepherd is Assistant Professor in the Department of History at Yale University. She received her Ph.D. in History from Harvard University. Before joining the Yale faculty, she was Junior Research Fellow in History at Trinity College, University of Cambridge. At Yale, Shepherd teaches courses on modern Japanese history, Korea and the Japanese Empire, and the history of colonial and imperial cities. Her book, The Narrowing Sea: Fukuoka, Pusan, and the Rise and Fall of an Imperial Region, came out in December 2025, from University of California Press. With Amy Stanley, she is currently working on co-translating and co-editing an English memoir of a former comfort woman, with the working title, The Life of Mun Ok Chu: a Korean woman's story of war and empire.

events.title: Laurent Warlouzet | Liberty, Solidarity and Community: Capitalism and European Integration, 1945 to the Present
events.description: How have European countries coped with the challenge of industrial capitalism and the rise of superpowers? Through an analysis of European integration from 1945 to the present day, Laurent Warlouzet argues that the European response was to create both new institutions, in particular the European Union, and an original framework of governance for capitalism. Beyond the European case, he demonstrates that capitalism is not just a contest between free marketeers and their opponents, those in favour of welfare and environmental policies, because there is a third camp that defends protectionism and assertive defence policies. Hence, the governance of capitalism has three foundational principles– liberty, solidarity, and community. The book explores debates among Europeans about how to address global interdependence in political, economic, and environmental terms. It is based on fresh archival evidence collected in eight countries. Laurent Warlouzet is professor of history at Paris Sorbonne Université. A former postdoctoral fellow at the London School of Economics (LSE) and at the European University Institute (EUI), he works on the international economic history of the post-1919 period, particularly European integration and comparative European history. His previous monograph in English (Governing Europe in a Globalizing World, 2018) was reviewed in Foreign Affairs. The book Liberty, Solidarity and Capitalism. European integration and capitalism is an updated version of Europe contre Europe, originally published in French and reviewed in the mainstream media, including Le Monde, Le Grand Continent and Mediapart. The book will be published in German by Hamburger and in Italian by Luiss UP. The book Liberty, Solidarity and Community is available in open-access on the Cambridge UP here (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/liberty-solidarity-and-community/355531CFEE184AFF8B706B24D25EC368). events.title: William Kentridge's The Head & the Load
events.location: Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts, Oakland
events.description: Thursday, November 12, 7:30pm Friday, November 13, 7:30pm Saturday, November 14, 7:30pm Sunday, November 15, 3pmTheater William Kentridge'sThe Head & the LoadWith music composed and conceived by Philip Miller with Thuthuka SibisiWilliam Kentridge, concept and director Philip Miller, composerGregory Maqoma, choreography Thuthuka Sibisi, music director and co-composer Visionary South African artist William Kentridge returns to Cal Performances after two previous visits, featuring the US premiere of SIBYL in 2023 and the Bay Area premiere of The Great Yes, The Great No in 2025. This time, he brings the West Coast premiere of a seminal work that—through dance, projection, speech, song, shadow play, costume, and music—chronicles the untold history of more than two million Africans who labored, fought, and died during the First World War. The Head & the Load takes its name from a Ghanaian proverb, "The head and the load are the troubles of the neck," and continues Kentridge's exploration of history, language, and artistic and political movements through richly layered and inventive performance works. Kentridge's production unfolds on a massive stage, weaving together texts by anticolonial authors and Dada poets in multiple languages, with original music by Philip Miller and Thuthuka Sibisi that intermingles traditional African songs with quotes from WWI-era European music by Satie, Hindemith, and Schoenberg.

events.title: Rahul Parson | Kathā-Kalkattā: Hindi Literature in a Bengali City
events.description: A talk by Rahul Parson (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/rahul-parson), Assistant Professor of Hindi Literature and Culture, at UC Berkeley, that recovers Calcutta as a major center of Hindi literary production from the 1950s to the 1990s, showing how its multilingual archives complicate conventional linguistic geographies of Indian literature and illuminate questions of migrancy, urban space, and literary recognition.Sukanya Banerjee (https://english.berkeley.edu/people/sukanya-banerjee), Associate Professor of English will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Mon, November 16, 2026 (NOTE NEW DATE) TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall —————- ABSTRACT Calcutta, Kolkata, Kalkattā: three names for one city, and the last one belongs to the Hindi and Urdu speakers who make up more than a third of its population. The conventional geography of Indian literature follows the linguistic boundaries drawn by the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 — literary habitations of Bengali for Bengal, Hindi for north India, Tamil for Tamil Nadu — a map that effaces Hindi writing produced outside the Hindi belt. Calcutta has been a Hindi literary city for over two centuries, since Bengal gave Hindi its first printed newspaper. This talk takes up the decades from the 1950s to the 1990s, when writers, editors, and theatre-makers set out to define what a Calcutta Hindi literature might be. They compiled their own archives, collections, and critical practices: R̥shi Jaiminī Kauśika's Kalakattā ke Hindī kathākāra (1952), Sharad Deora's two-volume Mahānagar (1969), the annual Kalkattā (1985–98), the journal Aṇimā, named for the yogic power of becoming infinitesimally small, and Shyamanand Jalan's theatre group Anamika. What emerged was a literature shaped by contact and separation at once — from Bengali locally, and from the movements of the Hindi belt. Reading the city as a literary confluence rather than a single tradition changes our account of both Hindi literature and Calcutta. The map was drawn over the multilingual city; the paper trail shows what it covered. The archive poses questions of migrancy, urban space, and literary recognition in Calcutta and similar global port cities. ABOUT THE SPEAKERRahul Parson (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/rahul-parson) received an MA and PhD in the Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley, with a specialization in Modern Hindi literature. Before returning to the Berkeley in 2021, he served as an Assistant Professor of Hindi and Urdu at the University of Colorado, Boulder (2016-2020) and a Wissenschaftlicher Mitarbeiter (Postdoctoral Researcher) at Max-Weber-Kolleg, Universität Erfurt, Germany (2014-2016). Rahul Parson's area of specialization is Hindi literature and literary history, with a particular emphasis on Hindi movements in Bengal. His book project, Confluences at the End of the Ganges: Modernity, Migration and Hindi Literature in Kolkata, fills in the Bengal portion of the map of Hindi studies. The monograph reveals the dynamism and syncretism of the hitherto overlooked world of Hindi literature in Bengal and the affective archives and narratives of migrants. It inaugurates research on the literatures of displaced and migrant peoples in South Asia by using cultural texts to explore the articulations of life-worlds of women and migrants. Additionally, he researches early-modern Jain poetry and philosophy, particularly the Jain adhyātma (spiritual or mystical) poetry. Dr. Parson participated as a core member of a research group based at the Max-Weber-Kolleg. In this capacity, he worked as a co-editor of a four-volume series entitled: Religious Individualisations: Historical Dimensions and Comparative Perspectives (Berlin: de Gruyter, 2020). events.title: The 2026 Emilio Segrè Lecture Featuring Francis Halzen: ICECUBE: Opening a Neutrino Window on the Universe from the South Pole
events.location: The Chevron Auditorium at International House
events.description: ICECUBE: Opening a Neutrino Window on the Universe from the South PoleFrancis Halzen, University of Wisconsin–Madison Abstract: The IceCube project at the South Pole melted 86 holes 2.5 kilometer deep in the Antarctic ice sheet to construct an enormous astronomical observatory that is also the largest neutrino detector ever built. The experiment discovered a flux of neutrinos from deep space with energies more than a million times those of neutrinos produced at accelerator laboratories like Fermilab. Some originate in the enigmatic cosmic particle accelerators that are the sources of cosmic rays. This lecture will discuss the IceCube neutrino telescope and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of cosmic origin. It will highlight the recent discovery that high-energy neutrinos—and cosmic rays—originate in sources powered by rotating supermassive black holes in active galaxies. With gravitational waves, high-energy gamma rays and neutrinos, IceCube launched multiparticle astronomy. Francis Halzen is a Vilas and Gregory Breit Distinguished Professor of Physics at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Born in Belgium, Halzen received his Master's and PhD degrees from the KU-Leuven, Belgium, and has been on the physics faculty at UW–Madison since 1972; in 2021, Halzen was named a Vilas Research Professor, one of the university's most prestigious honors. He has been a fellow of the American Physical Society since 1994 and a member of the US National Academy since 2024, and is the recipient of numerous awards, including the 2014 Smithsonian American Ingenuity Award, the 2015 Balzan Prize, a 2018 Bruno Pontecorvo Prize, the 2019 IUPAP Yodh Prize, the 2021 Bruno Rossi Prize, the 2021 Homi Bhabha Award, and honorary doctorates at several universities. Halzen is the Principal Investigator of IceCube, a cubic-kilometer neutrino telescope buried in the Antarctic ice at the South Pole. IceCube's first observations of high-energy cosmic neutrinos garnered the 2013 Physics World Breakthrough of the Year Award. In September 2017, IceCube detected a high-energy neutrino from the direction of a blazar called TXS 0506+056. This was the first-ever evidence of a source of high-energy cosmic rays, whose origins have been notoriously difficult to pinpoint since they were discovered over one hundred years ago. Also a skilled science communicator, Halzen travels widely, giving about 20 or more invited talks per year at conferences, workshops, and colloquia. He also gives regular public talks to local and national groups and interviews for television and radio. Halzen is the co-author of Quarks and Leptons, a classic textbook on modern particle physics that continues to be used extensively throughout college campuses today. He has a large number of publications to his credit and has written or edited several other books. His essay "Antarctic Dreams," about the early days of AMANDA, IceCube's precursor, was featured in The Best American Science Writing 2000.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Founders and Their Heterogeneous Firms"
events.description: Abstract: Firm creation is at the heart of macroeconomic growth, but entrepreneurial outcomes are highly unequal. In this paper, we study the determinants of which entrants become large firms with macroeconomic importance. Using employer-employee-shareholder linked Canadian administrative data based on tax records, we find that workers with higher employment earnings are more likely both to enter entrepreneurship and to found larger firms with greater growth potential. We incorporate this link between founders' labor-market and entrepreneurial capacities into a quantitative model of endogenous occupational choice. In the presence of ex-ante heterogeneity, small business tax deductions induce negative selection by drawing lower-potential entrepreneurs into entry, largely oﬀsetting their positive eﬀects in alleviating financial frictions and generating a quantity-quality trade-oﬀ in the design of entrepreneurial policies.

events.title: Aditya Balasubramanian | Crossings Interrupted or Invisibilized? Rethinking Migration Across the Bay of Bengal
events.description: A talk by Aditya Balasubramanian (https://researchers.anu.edu.au/researchers/balasubramanian-a), Senior Lecturer in History at the Australian National University, drawing on a rare archive of family letters and remittances to examine the understudied history of Indian middle-class migration to Southeast Asia and the ways the Depression shaped mobility, economic insecurity, social isolation, and transimperial connections to home. Event moderated by Matthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer), Assistant Professor of History at UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Tue, Nov 17, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————–ABSTRACT: Studies of migration across the Bay of Bengal focus largely on the movement of millions of Tamil labourers between the second half of the 19th century and the 1930s to serve the demands of British imperial capital accumulation during the first era of globalization. While connected histories of South and Southeast Asia and memory point to "a large middling group of Indians, clerks in government and private offices, doctors, drivers, lower management in the oilwells and teak sawmills," shopkeepers, and traders (Bayly and Harper, 2005), they fail to say very much about this class of people because of their invisibility to the colonial archive. This paper begins to illuminate what has been hidden thus far. It draws chiefly on the author's collection of 500 pages of remittances and correspondences exchanged between his maternal grandfather P.K. "Java" Raman (1909-97) who migrated to work as a typist in Batavia (today's Jakarta) in the Dutch East Indies and his family members in the Malabar region of British India, between 1930 and 1934. The paper suggests the Depression as a period of migration rather than its eclipse; explores structures of feeling around economic insecurity and isolation of the thin stratum of Indian professionals in Southeast Asia; and sketches an earlier history of remittance between Indians overseas and in the homeland, across empires. Looking beyond the letters, it discusses possible sources and themes for microhistories of crossing the Bay of Bengal.ABOUT THE SPEAKER:Aditya Balasubramanian (https://researchers.anu.edu.au/researchers/balasubramanian-a) is a Senior Lecturer at ANU's School of History, in the College of Arts and Social Sciences (CASS). Aditya's first book, Toward a Free Economy: Swatantra and Opposition Politics in Democratic India (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2023), is a history of economic ideas and politics (UK/US link (https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691205243/toward-a-free-economy) South Asia link (https://www.amazon.in/Toward-Free-Economy-Swatantra-Opposition/dp/0691256578)). It was shortlisted for the 2022 Elder Prize in the Social Sciences of the American Institute of Indian Studies and the 2024 W.K. Hancock Prize for best first monograph of the Australian Historical Association, and longlisted for the 2024 Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay Prize of the New India Foundation. A suite of peer-reviewed articles published over the last several years have interrogated various aspects of Indian political economy between the 1940s and the 1970s. Topics range from India's role in the international economic order, famine in Travancore during World War II, Hindu nationalist economic thought and policy, and anticorruption. He is currently working on two projects. The first is an environmental and economic history of roadbuilding and transport in India. Initial thoughts appeared in this post (https://histecon.fas.harvard.edu/climate-loss/roads/index.html) for the Harvard Center for History and Economics' "Visualizing Climate and Loss" blog in October 2023. During 2025-2028, he is the recipient of an Australian Research Council Discovery Early Career Research Award (DECRA) for this project. The second is a synthetic history of the Bhopal Gas Tragedy of 1984, the world's largest industrial disaster. This project is especially concerned with failures of relief and rehabilitation, chronic illnesses, and ongoing environmental pollution. He has just completed an article on forest management in India and is working on an article that sketches a revisionist history of migration between South and Southeast Asia. At ANU, Aditya teaches or has taught historical methods, environmental history, the history of political economy, and South Asian history. His teaching has been recognized with nominations for College and University-wide prizes. He is the Deputy Director of ANU's Center for Environmental History (https://history.cass.anu.edu.au/centres/ceh) and founded the ANU Capitalism Studies Network (http://csn.anu.edu.au/) with Will Bateman (Law) and Melinda Cooper (Sociology). He is completing a second term as Board Member of the South Asia Research Institute (2020-2021, 2024-6). From 2018 to 2024, he created and coordinated the Archives of Economic Life in South and Southeast Asia (https://www.histecon.magd.cam.ac.uk/archives-asia/index.html) website (you can learn more about it in this (https://toynbeeprize.org/posts/doing-online-south-southeast-asian-history/) Toynbee Prize Blog interview). events.title: Bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā - Not a moonless night: Śamathadeva's Upāyikā, the oral life of Mūlasarvāstivāda scripture, and early Buddhist philology
events.description: An exposition of the Abhidharma without the Āgamas, however flawless, "does not capture the heart, just like a moonless night." So runs the colophon of Śamathadeva's Abhidharmakośopāyikā-ṭīkā (Upāyikā for short), a monumental Sanskrit commentary now extant only in Tibetan translation. The Upāyikā is a commentary of an unusual kind. Rather than explaining Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya through standard exegetical procedures, it traces its scriptural citations back to their authoritative canonical settings in the Āgamas, often reproducing extensive passages, some of which do not otherwise survive in the received corpora. The same colophon states that these canonical materials were recalled from memory. Taking this seriously, the lecture will treat the Upāyikā both as a companion reader to the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya and as a witness to the oral textual life of the contemporaneous Mūlasarvāstivāda lineages of recitation in India. It will examine how the scriptures available to Śamathadeva were organized and transmitted, and will try to locate the otherwise unknown figure of Śamathadeva in time and space. Close philological engagement with this text will show what the practice of early Buddhist philology has to say about what counts as a text and as text-historical evidence.Bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā is a Visiting Associate Research Professor in the Department of Buddhist Sudies at Dharma Drum Institute of Liberal Arts (Taiwan), Director of the Āgama Research Group, and currently the Numata Visiting Professor for Buddhist Studies at the University of California at Berkeley. link (https://bhikkhunidhammadinna.com/)

events.title: Berkeley Book Chat with Ignacio Navarrete
events.description: In Sneaking into Print (Toronto, 2026), Ignacio Navarrete (Spanish & Portuguese) explores the impact of early printing on narrative literature in Spain. He reveals how new technology enabled older texts and translations to circulate alongside newly written works, giving rise to a distinct narrative culture. Through an in-depth study of various narrative subgenres including hagiography, the epic, and sentimental fiction, Sneaking into Print integrates historical bibliography, material book features, and literary analysis. By examining texts as physical artifacts and narrative constructs, the book sheds light on their broader implications for narrative theory, offering fresh perspectives on the intersections of literature, materiality, and the early print marketplace. Navarrete is joined by Nicholas Paige (French). After a brief discussion, they respond to questions from the audience.

events.title: International Court of Justice: Judicial Fellowship Panel
events.description: ICJ Judicial Fellowship Panel Wednesday, November 18 · 1:00 PM · Berkeley Law, Room 141 Each year, the International Court of Justice selects fifteen Judicial Fellows from hundreds of candidates nominated by law schools around the world to clerk at the Peace Palace in The Hague for ten months. Berkeley Law nominates up to four candidates each year and provides a significant fellowship stipend for any Berkeley nominee the Court selects. Join BJIL and ILS, with support from the Miller Institute, for a conversation with four recent Judicial Fellows: Félix Aguettant (Berkeley Law LL.M. ’23), Allyson Ping, Lara Manbeck, and Marina Wilbraham. They will talk about the application process, their time at the Court, and where the fellowship has taken them since. PANELISTS Félix Aguettant is a lawyer in the Legal Service of the European Commission, in the EU External Relations and International Law team, based in Brussels. He is also a PhD candidate in public international law at the Sorbonne. He was a 2024-25 Judicial Fellow for H.E. Judge Abraham and H.E. President Iwasawa. He is an alumnus of Berkeley Law’s executive LLM program and was nominated to the fellowship by Berkeley Law in 2024. He is currently the head coach of Berkeley Law’s 2026-27 Jessup team. Félix is bilingual in English and French and is a member of the California Bar. To date, Felix is the only Berkeley Law alum to have ever been a judicial fellow! Allyson Ping is a litigation associate at Debevoise & Plimpton, New York. From 2024-2025, she served as a Judicial Fellow to H.E. President Iwasawa Yuji. Allyson received a J.D. from Columbia Law School in 2024, where she was a member of the Jessup Moot Court team and was co-Executive Editor of the Columbia Journal of Transnational Law. Lara Manbeck is an Associate at Covington & Burling in Washington, D.C. From 2025 to 2026, she served as a Judicial Fellow to H.E. Judge Nolte and later as an Associate Legal Officer at the Court. She received her J.D. from Columbia Law School, where she served as Editor-in-Chief of the Columbia Journal of Transnational Law, an MPhil from the University of Cambridge, and a B.A. from New York University. Prior to law school, she worked in the Office of the Director-General of the International Development Law Organization. Marina Wilbraham is currently a Law Clerk at White and Case LLP, in the firm’s LA office, where her practice focuses on international technology disputes. She was a 2025-2026 Judicial Fellow for H.E. Judge Sarah H. Cleveland. Previously, she was an Associate at Debevoise & Plimpton LLP for two years in New York, in the Litigation Department, where she worked on a mix of international arbitration, public international law, and commercial litigation matters. Marina is a 2023 Yale Law School graduate. BERKELEY LAW’S JUDICIAL FELLOWSHIP APPLICATIONS Applications for the 2027–28 judicial fellowship, run by the CDO, will open in December 2026 and close in January 2027. Details about the 2026-27 application for Berkeley Law’s nomination process here. You can find details about the fellowship on the ICJ Judicial Fellowship website. JD and LL.M. students in the classes of 2025, 2026 and 2027 are eligible to apply, provided they meet other eligibility criteria of the Court. LUNCH Lunch will be provided if you RSVP here.

events.description: Events Add to Calendar iCal / Outlook The US nuclear weapons complex is undergoing its biggest transformation since the end of the Cold War. Increasingly sophisticated experimental, computational, and manufacturing techniques that emerged to support a strategy of science-based stockpile stewardship are now being applied as tools for vertical proliferation as emphasis shifts from ‘stewardship’ to production. The evolution of laboratory tools for weapons development comes with both challenges and opportunities for verification, nonproliferation, and disarmament. This talk will address the paradigm shift underway in the US and its implications for new plutonium pit production and the potential resumption of nuclear testing.

events.title: Katherine Nagel: Understanding the logic of the fly navigation system
events.description: All animals need to navigate to find food and resources in their environment. My lab has been using odor-guided navigation to uncover the organization and logic of the fly navigation system. I will present recent and ongoing work aiming to describe how the fan-shaped body, a part of the fly navigation system thought to specify allocentric goal directions, organizes multi-sensory input and computes goals based on ongoing experience. One of our guiding interests is understanding what is similar and different across the navigation systems of different species. I hope this question inspires some interesting discussions!

events.title: Esha Niyogi De | Women's Transborder Cinema: Authorship, Stardom, and Filmic Labor in South Asia
events.description: A talk by Esha Niyogi De (https://wp.ucla.edu/person/esha-niyogi-de/), Senior Lecturer in UCLA's Writing Programs, on her new book, Women's Transborder Cinema: Authorship, Stardom, and Filmic Labor in South Asia (https://www.press.uillinois.edu/books/?id=p088285) (University of Illinois Press, December 2024). The book uncovers the overlooked histories of women who worked as producers, directors, performers, and "star-authors" across the film industries of India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. De examines how these women used stardom, collaboration, and creative labor to cross geographic, institutional, and gendered boundaries, claim greater authority over filmmaking, and challenge the structures that often obscured their contributions to South Asian cinema.Maya Sidhu (https://french.berkeley.edu/people/maya-sidhu), Lecturer in the Department of French and a scholar of film and media studies, will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies; Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies, UC Berkeley. This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter). ————–DATE: Thu, November 19, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter) ————– ABOUT THE BOOK This book talk delves into previously submerged histories and hidden voices of women directors and film entrepreneurs from Bangladesh, Pakistan, and India. Drawing on neglected archives and rare field interviews with filmmakers and fans, Esha tells a comparative story of women's creative authority and entrepreneurial labor in selected film industries of South Asia—industries and markets that share languages, arts, and geopolitical rifts. Using "transborder" to refer not only to territorial borders but also to institutional and conceptual ones, her story dwells on two eras of women's cinema in this postcolonial region. In the era of the "star-authors" (50s-90s), female stars in Dhaka, Lahore, and Kolkata perform personas ambiguously to access infrastructures and direct fiction films that breach sexual and national borders. In the era of the "woman director" (2000s), even though opportunities appear to burgeon across the region, women negotiate transnational borders that take less obvious forms of brand-making and censorship. The talk will include rare footage from fiction films made by Kohinoor Akhtar Suchanda, Babita, Nargis Akhter (Bangladesh), Shamim Ara (Pakistan), and Kanan Devi (India). SPEAKER BIOEsha Niyogi De (https://wp.ucla.edu/person/esha-niyogi-de/)'s research interests lie in South Asian gender politics, film and performance history, and literary history. She is the author of two monographs, a recent study of women's cinemas in selected film industries of Bangladesh, Pakistan, and India titled Women's Transborder Cinema: Authorship, Stardom, and Filmic Labor in South Asia (University of Illinois Press, 2024), and an earlier book on sexual politics and postcoloniality in literature, cinema, and choreography in the Bengal region titled Empire, Media, and the Autonomous Woman: A Feminist Critique of Postcolonial Thought (Oxford University Press, 2011). Other publications include two co-edited books, from University of Washington Press and Duke University Press, and many articles. She is working on two new book projects. The first, a study of the renowned Pakistani actress-singer and film director Noor Jehan in relation to Muslim nationalist arts in the mid-twentieth century, is titled Recasting Noor Jehan:Melody Queen, Film Pioneer, and the Making of National Cultures in South Asia (co-authored with Gwendolyn Sarah Kirk). The second, a comparative study of gendered choreographies of protest in twentieth century avant-garde and industrial films, made by Zahir Raihan, Satyajit Ray, Rangeela, among others, is tentatively titled Moving Bodies Out of Line: Filmic Choreographies, Protest Movements, and Queerness in South Asian Cinemas. Esha is a Senior Lecturer in the Division of Writing Programs at UCLA and a Faculty Affiliate of the UCLA Center for India and South Asia.EVENT POSTER _____________ Established in 2013 with a generous gift from the Subir & Malini Chowdhury Foundation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subir_Chowdhury), The Subir & Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies (https://chowdhurycenter.berkeley.edu/) at UC Berkeley champions the study of Bangladesh's cultures, peoples and history. The first of its kind in the US, the Center's mission is to create an innovative model combining research, scholarships, the promotion of art and culture, and the building of ties between institutions in Bangladesh and the University of California. Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/The-Subir-Malini-Chowdhury-Center-for-Bangladesh-Studies-752426458213022/?ref=hl) For DIRECTIONS to the Institute please enter "Institute for South Asia Studies" in your google maps or click this GOOGLE MAPS LINK (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+10+Stephens+Hall,+Berkeley,+CA+94720/@37.8710692,-122.2585002,19z/data=!4m16!1m7!3m6!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2sInstitute+for+South+Asia+Studies!3b1!8m2!3d37.8710952!4d-122.2576645!4m7!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952).PARKING INFORMATION (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/parking-around-campus)Please note that parking is not always easily available in Berkeley. events.title: [ASP] In-Person Practice Exam
events.description: Taking a practice exam is one of the best ways to prepare for law school exams! Practice helps you get comfortable with your skills and identify what you should prioritize as you study. The ASP is providing an opportunity to practice taking a law school exam under simulated exam conditions. You should bring your laptop and a practice exam (ideally, a three- or four-hour exam). You must bring your own practice exam; no exam will be provided. Whether you should bring your outline and notes depends on whether you will have access to those materials on your exams. The point of the exercise is to simulate actual exam conditions. Resources for finding practice exams are available on the Academic Skills Program website. The practice exam does not need to be from your professor so long as the form of the question is the same. If you haven’t finished reviewing and outlining, you should still take a practice exam, but consider taking it open book. Use the practice exam as an opportunity to start learning the material. Looking for more information and support? You can schedule a meeting with us here: BerkeleyLawASP.as.me.

events.title: Probabilistic Operator Algebra Seminar: Real Infinitesimal Freeness of Wigner Matrices
events.location: to attend via Zoom email David Jekel (djekel@uottawa.ca) remote on-line talk
events.description: Speaker: Samuel Gurrola Viramontes, CIMAT GuanajatoIn this talk, within the framework of real infinitesimal free probability introduced by Cebron and Mingo, we will discuss the calculation of the real infinitesimal free cumulants of independent complex Wigner matrices. Our approach relies on establishing a combinatorial relation between annular non-crossing partitions and families of directed graphs. As a consequence, we show that independent complex Wigner matrices are asymptotically real infinitesimally free. In particular, under mild conditions, a complex Wigner matrix is asymptotically infinitesimally free from its transpose. This is based on joint work with James A. Mingo (arXiv:2609.24023).

events.title: Authors Meet Critics: "Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis"
events.description: Please join us on Tuesday, November 24th from 4:00–5:30pm for an Authors Meet Critics panel on the book Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis by Matthew Shutzer, Assistant Professor of History at UC Berkeley. Professor Shutzer will be joined in conversation by Youjin Chung, Associate Professor in the Department of Environmental Science, Policy & Management and the Energy & Resources Group at UC Berkeley, and Daniel Aldana Cohen, Assistant Professor of Sociology at UC Berkeley. The talk will be moderated by Michael Watts, Class of '63 and Chancellor's Professor of Geography Emeritus and Co-Director of Development Studies at UC Berkeley. This event is co-sponsored by the UC Berkeley Departments of South & Southeast Asia Studies and Geography, and the Energy and Resources Group.About the Book India is today one of the world's largest producers and consumers of fossil fuels, driving new investments in the global fossil economy and achieving record-breaking levels of coal extraction at home. As the planet burns from climate change, this entrenchment of fossil fuel dependence has left many searching for how we arrived at this point. Until the Last Ton provides a sweeping new appraisal of this planetary dilemma, uncovering how India became part of an emerging fossil capitalism that continues to shape the present. In the book, Matthew Shutzer recasts the origins of the fossil economy by showing how European industrialization unleashed a global search for fossil energy in the colonial world. Placing India at the center of this history, Shutzer traces how the highland forests of eastern India became early frontiers for global coal investment, transforming this landscape into the largest site of imperial overseas coal production across a century of colonial rule. At the heart of these shifts was a legal framework of subterranean property, which redefined local relations of land ownership and social power, while tying the growth of India's fossil economy to the progressive ecological destruction of the forest frontier. Following these dynamics into the postcolonial period, Until the Last Ton reveals the enduring impacts of colonial property on independent India's energy history, shedding new light on postwar struggles for energy development and resource sovereignty, as well as the violent conflicts over mining dispossession that have haunted India's economic ascent in an age of climate crisis.PanelistsMatthew Shutzer (https://history.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/current/matthew-shutzer) is an environmental historian of South Asia. His research and teaching are concerned with the place of the environment in global history, with a particular focus on fossil fuels, agriculture, forests, climate change, and environmental politics. He has also worked on topics that connect global environmental history to histories of law, capitalism, post-colonial development, the earth sciences, and photography. His book, Until the Last Ton: Fossil Fuels in India from Empire to the Climate Crisis, is the first history of fossil fuels in colonial and post-colonial South Asia. He is currently at work on a second book project on climate change and the making of the Third World after 1945.Youjin B. Chung (https://youjinbchung.net/about) studies the relationship between gender and inequality, rural development, and socio-environmental change in East Africa, with a focus on Tanzania. The overarching question that drives her research program is: how and why do development policies and processes that aim to improve sustainability and equity outcomes often reinforce existing power structures and marginalize the groups they intend to serve? Over the years, she has channeled this central animating concern into three specific research projects. Using Tanzania as an analytic case, these projects investigate some of the most contentious issues in global development and environmental politics: large-scale farmland investments, sustainable livestock intensification, and the critical minerals rush. She is the author of Sweet Deal, Bitter Landscape: Gender Politics and Liminality in Tanzania's New Enclosures (Cornell University Press, 2024). At Berkeley, she convenes the Critical Ruralities Lab, a research workshop and collaborative mentoring space that promotes empirically grounded and justice-oriented scholarship on development and socio-environmental change in the global countryside.Daniel Aldana Cohen (https://aldanacohen.com/) is Assistant Professor of Sociology at the University of California, Berkeley, where he is Director of the Socio-Spatial Climate Collaborative, or (SC)2 (https://sc2.berkeley.edu/), and serves as a faculty affiliate in the graduate program on Political Economy. He is also Founding Co-Director of the Climate and Community Institute, a progressive climate and economy think tank. He has been a CIFAR Azrieli Global Scholar (2021-24) and Member of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey (2018-19). He is the co-author of A Planet to Win: Why We Need a Green New Deal (Verso 2019). Cohen works on the intersections of the climate emergency, housing, political economy, social movements, and inequalities of race and class in the United States and Brazil. As Director of (SC)2, he is leading qualitative and quantitative research projects on Whole Community Climate Mapping, green political economy, and eco-apartheid. He was also co-founder and co-PI of the Superstorm Research Lab (https://superstormresearchlab.org/), in New York City.Michael Watts (https://geography.berkeley.edu/professor-emeritus-michael-watts) is Class of '63 and Chancellor's Professor of Geography Emeritus and Co-Director of Development Studies at UC Berkeley. He served as the Director of the Institute of International Studies at Berkeley from 1994 to 2004 and was Director of Social Science Matrix at Berkeley in 2019–20. He was most recently a Non-resident Long-term Fellow at the Swedish Collegium for Advanced Study (SCAS). Watts is a member of the British Academy, was a Guggenheim Fellow in 2003, and was awarded the Victoria Medal by the Royal Geographical Society in 2004, and the Berlin Prize by the American Academy in Berlin in 2016. He was awarded the Ester Boserup Prize in 2024. Watts' writing has addressed a number of development issues especially famine and food security, political violence and the agrarian question in Africa, South Asia and Vietnam, natural resources and especially the energy and mineral sectors, and the political economy of development and governance, more generally. Watts has worked for UNDP, OECD and other development organizations, including the Ford, Rockefeller and MacArthur Foundations. He has published over fifteen books and three hundred articles and has worked extensively with the renowned photographer Ed Kashi. Watts has written extensively on the oil industry, extractive economies and international commodity trading firms.

events.description: CRG Forum SeriesBook TalkEvery Man’s Home a Castle: Parental Rights and the Makings of Modern ConservatismwithJulia Bowes, Lecturer in gender history at the University of Melbourne, and author of Every Man's Home a Castle: Parental Rights and the Makings of Modern Conservatism (Princeton University Press, 2026) Dr. JuliaBowes is a lecturer in gender history at the University of Melbourne, where her research focuses on the relationship between gender, the family, and conservatism in the United States. Her first book, Every Man's Home a Castle: Parental Rights and the Makings of Modern Conservatism (Princeton University Press, 2026), examines how a sovereign conception of the white patriarchal family was at the crux of an emerging conservative ideology opposed to the modern liberal state. The book is an extended version of her dissertation, which was awarded the 2019 Lerner-Scott Prize for the best dissertation in US women's history by the Organization of American Historians. She has held fellowships from the Jefferson Scholars Foundation, the Institute of Citizens and Scholars (formerly the Woodrow Wilson Institute), and, prior to joining the University of Melbourne, was an assistant professor at the University of Hong Kong. She is now researching a project on the gendered politics of alternative health movements, including anti-vaccination, anti-fluoridation, and home birth movements, in the twentieth-century United States. *If you require an accommodation for effective communication (ASL interpreting/CART captioning, alternative media formats, etc.) to fully participate in this event, please contact Ariana Ceja at centerrg@berkeley.edu with as much advance notice as possible and at least 7-10 days in advance of the event.

events.title: Student Faculty Macro Lunch: "Importing Aggregate Demand"
events.description: Abstract: How exposed are open economies to global demand shocks? In equilibrium, foreign booms can be absorbed either by domestic consumption ("quantities") or by real exchange rate appreciation ("prices"). We show that failures of Ricardian equivalence and global financial market imperfections, two frictions popular in much recent work, have opposite effects on the split: while elevated marginal propensities to consume push towards quantities, financial frictions instead increase price adjustment. As the flexible-price equilibrium generally features a mix of quantity and price responses, policy needs to be contractionary to achieve flexible-price outcomes if the spending effect dominates, and vice-versa if financial frictions are severe. In our quantitative explorations the spending effect tends to win the race, necessitating aggressive domestic policy action.

events.title: Book Talk: An Anticolonial Development: Race, Schooling, and Emancipation in Twentieth-Century West Africa
events.description: Book Talk:An Anticolonial Development: Race, Schooling, and Emancipation in Twentieth-Century West Africa (Cambridge University Press, 2026) In what measure could education be an agent of African freedom? Combining histories of race, economics, and education, Elisa Prosperetti examines this question in two West African contexts, Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire, from the 1890s to the 1980s. She argues that a Black Atlantic perspective changes how we see decolonization and development in West Africa, by revealing schooling's essential role in aspirations of African emancipation. Rejecting colonial exploitation of the African body, proponents of anticolonial development instead claimed the mind as the site of economic productivity for African people. An Anticolonial Development shows how, in the middle of the twentieth century, Africans proposed an original understanding of development that fused antiracism to economic theory, and human dignity to material productivity. Elisa Prosperetti is an Assistant Professor of History at the National Institute of Education/Nanyang Technological University, Singapore. She is a historian of modern African and global history, specializing in histories of race, development, education, and decolonization, with a geographic focus on West Africa and the Black Atlantic world. She received her PhD in History from Princeton University in 2020, and currently serves on the Editorial Review Board of the African Studies Review and as a podcast host for the African Studies channel of the New Books Network.

events.title: Harjant S. Gill | Coming of Age in Macholand: Masculinity, Patriarchy, and the Search for Freedom in Indian Punjab
events.description: Join us for a book launch and signing by Harjant S. Gil (https://www.towson.edu/cla/departments/socioanthrocrim/facultystaff/hgill.html)l, Professor of Anthropology at Towson University and an award-winning documentary filmmaker, based on his new book, Coming of Age in Macholand: Masculinity, Patriarchy, and the Search for Freedom in Indian Punjab (https://www.harjantgill.com/coming-of-age-in-macholand) (University of Chicago Press, forthcoming in Nov 2026), an eye-opening examination of masculinity, violence, and transnational migration focused on present-day Indian Punjab. Pre-order the book now. Only limited copies will be available to purchase at the event" - https://www.harjantgill.com/coming-of-age-in-macholand (https://www.harjantgill.com/coming-of-age-in-macholand). Event moderated by Lawrence Cohen (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/lawrence-cohen), Professor of Anthropology and of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Chair, Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Co-Director, Medical Anthropology Program, UC Berkeley. ���———–DATE: Tue, Dec 1, 2026 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ————– ABOUT THE BOOKIn Coming of Age in Macholand (https://www.harjantgill.com/coming-of-age-in-macholand), anthropologist and filmmaker Harjant Gill examines how Punjabi men in India, disillusioned by promises of power and control, contend with patriarchy: by submitting to it, attempting to transgress it, migrating to escape it, or coming undone by it. Gill takes readers deep inside men's worlds to show how boys come of age and how masculinity is produced through pervasive violence, while also being underwritten by intimacy, fraternal love, and homosocial bonds. Based on four years of fieldwork conducted over a decade and hundreds of interviews, Gill explores how boys learn to become men against the backdrop of patriarchal constraints, political violence, shifting agrarian economies, and steady outward migration. He shows the extent to which violence is a function and a reflection of powerlessness. By tracing the making of masculinity in a society where sexuality is sanctioned almost exclusively through heteronormative frameworks of marriage and family, this book documents how patriarchy forecloses agency and autonomy. Ultimately, Coming of Age in Macholand offers a powerful indictment of patriarchy as a system that not only oppresses women and queer people, but also constricts men's intimate, sexual, and emotional lives. ABOUT THE AUTHORHarjant Gill (https://www.towson.edu/cla/departments/socioanthrocrim/facultystaff/hgill.html) is a professor of anthropology and an award-winning documentary filmmaker whose work bridges ethnography, visual storytelling, and public scholarship. His research and creative practice explore masculinity, migration, media, religion, and popular culture in South Asia and its diasporas, with a particular focus on Punjab and Sikh communities. Through film and writing, he examines how intimate lives are shaped by patriarchy, nationalism, violence, and transnational mobility. Gill is the director of the internationally recognized documentary films Roots of Love, Mardistan/Macholand, and Sent Away Boys. His work has been broadcast on the BBC, PBS, and Doordarshan and screened widely at universities, film festivals, and public forums around the world. His scholarship appears in leading journals including American Anthropologist, Ethnography, and Visual Anthropology Review. His forthcoming book, Coming of Age in Macholand (University of Chicago Press), offers a deeply personal ethnographic exploration of patriarchy, masculinity, violence, and migration in Indian Punjab. Gill has received fellowships and awards from the American Institute of Indian Studies, Fulbright-Nehru, Point Foundation, Wenner-Gren, Whiting, and Woodrow Wilson foundations. Born in Chandigarh (India), Gill grew up in SF Bay Area and now lives in Washington, DC. events.title: PMB Seminar with Vivian Irish | Thorny questions: citrus development and disease
events.description: Thorns are plant defensive structures that arise from axillary shoot apical meristems that proliferate for a time and then terminally differentiate into a sharp hard tip. Like other meristems, thorn meristems contain stem cells but, in the case of thorns, these stem cells undergo a programmed cessation of proliferative activity. Using citrus as a model system to examine this unusual form of stem cell regulation, we have characterized a transcriptional gene network necessary for thorn development. Not only has this work illuminated some of the molecular mechanisms controlling plant stem cell activity, but the methods we have developed have allowed us to tackle some of the challenges facing citrus agriculture today.

events.title: Amara Ali | Beyond Delhi and Lucknow: The Lives of Urdu in Twentieth-Century Kashmir
events.description: A talk by Amara Ali, (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/amara-ali) Lecturer in Urdu, Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley, that examines twentieth-century Kashmir as a distinctive center of Urdu literary culture through the evolution of Shia marṣiya.Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. ————–DATE: Thu, December 3, 2026 (NEW DATE) TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall —————- ABSTRACT The history of Urdu has largely been told through its major centers, Delhi and Lucknow, with other regions positioned as peripheral recipients of a tradition formed elsewhere. This talk turns to Kashmir to complicate that geography, taking the twentieth century as its focus. This was a period in which Kashmir developed its own robust institutions of Urdu literary production and appreciation, from madrasas and administrative offices to mushāʿira gatherings and radio broadcasts. Multilingualism has long been part and parcel of Kashmiri intellectual and cultural life, with different languages holding prominence in different periods: Sanskrit, then Persian, and eventually Urdu. To trace how this played out in the twentieth century, the talk turns to Kashmiri Shia marṣiya, a devotional genre, and its jadīd (modern) forms, which register this movement between languages and make visible Kashmir's own productive engagement with Urdu. SPEAKER BIOAmara Ali (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/amara-ali) is a Lecturer in the Department of South and Southeast Asian Studies. Her research centers on the interplay of Urdu, Hindi, and Kashmiri literary traditions and Islam in South Asia. Her doctoral dissertation provides a literary examination of the Kashmiri marsiya (an elegiac poem), analyzing how this local form articulates a unique Kashmiri aesthetic, while remaining in critical dialogue with the broader Urdu, Persian, and Arabic literary traditions. Earlier, she completed her master's studies at the University of Cambridge, focusing on the celebrated Urdu poets Mirza Ghalib and Faiz Ahmed Faiz.Event Poster —————— Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. events.title: Reactionary Politics in South Korea: Historical Legacies, Far-Right Intellectuals, and Political Mobilization
events.location: Institute of East Asian Studies, Conference Room, 2111 Bancroft Way, 5th Floor, Berkeley, CA 94720
events.description: Speaker: Myungji Yang (University of Hawai'i, Mānoa) Hybrid Event | RSVP/Registration Required RSVP for In Person Attendance at Bottom of Page Register for Virtual Attendance - COMING SOON Note: This event will begin on "Berkeley Time" at 5:10 PM. Talk Summary: The rise of the illiberal, far-right politics threatens democratic system throughout the world. The South Korean president Yoon Seok-yeol's martial law declaration in December 2024 stunned the world. More puzzling is that Yoon's insurrection unexpectedly gained substantial support from the ruling right-wing party and ordinary citizens. Why do ordinary citizens support authoritarian leaders and martial law in a democratic country? What draws these citizens to extreme actions and ideas? Through eighteen months of field research and drawing from rich qualitative data, this talk will provide an in-depth account of the ideas and practices of the far-right groups and organizations, and help to understand the roots of current democratic regression. Speaker Bio: Myungji Yang is Professor of Sociology at the University of Hawai'i-Mānoa. A political sociologist and social movement scholar, she is interested in the issues of power, inequality, civil society and democracy. Her research has appeared in Nations and Nationalism, Politics and Society, Mobilization: An International Inquiry, Urban Studies, and Sociological Inquiry, among other venues. She is the author of two books, From Miracle to Mirage (2018, Cornell University Press) and Reactionary Politics in South Korea: Historical Legacies, Far-Right Intellectuals, and Political Mobilization (2026, Cambridge University Press). She is currently developing a research project on young men's radicalization and anti-feminist politics.

events.title: 2027 Sheng Yen Conference
events.description: The scholastic traditions associated with Sarvāstivāda and the Abhidharma corpus more broadly were transmitted to China beginning in the fourth and fifth centuries and became a significant focus of translation activity under the direction of Xuanzang in the seventh century. Yet modern scholarship often assumes that Chinese Buddhist scholiasts had little sustained interest in, or use for, Abhidharma. According to this view, Abhidharma was dismissed as "Hīnayāna" and overshadowed by the rise of indigenous Chinese Buddhist traditions such as Chan, Tiantai, and Huayan. There is, however, ample evidence that Abhidharma continued to be studied and valued by Chinese exegetes irrespective of their doctrinal or school affiliation, and that it retained an important place in monastic curricula from the medieval period down to the present day. This conference seeks to reconsider the reception and enduring influence of Abhidharma in Chinese Buddhism.Titles, Abstracts, and Bios (https://events.berkeley.edu/live/files/66-titles-abstracts-and-biospdf).Friday 2:30-5:30 pmAbhidharma Learning in China Chair: Alexander von Rospatt Eric Greene (Yale University): "Abhidharma Methodology in the First Era of Chinese Buddhist Scholasticism." events.title: Shiben Banerji | Object, Site, Antecedent, Exemplar: India in the Occult Imagination of the Globe
events.description: A talk by Shiben Banerji, (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/shiben-banerji) Associate Professor of Architecture and Urbanism, History of Art Department, at UC Berkeley. ——–DATE: Thu, Mar 4, 2027 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall Event live streamed on FB at ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley) ��———- SPEAKER BIOShiben Banerji (https://arthistory.berkeley.edu/people/shiben-banerji) is Associate Professor in the Dept of History of Art. He interested in the rhetorical and performative dimensions of architecture. His classroom teaching and historical scholarship are animated by three questions. First, how did architects in early modern Europe describe their interest in the nature of political oratory at the very moment that they began studying architectural forms that were not derived from Roman antiquity? Second, how did architects across the Americas, Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australia mediate new conceptions of public association in the context of nineteenth-century colonialisms, and how did concomitant experiments in old and new media present architectural and urban space as objects of artistic depiction and literary invention? Third, how did twentieth-century theorists of alternatives to liberal modernity in the ex-colonial world conceptualize the work of architectural media in altering perception and consciousness? Shiben is the author of Lineages of the Global City(link is external) (University of Texas Press, 2025), which was supported by a Mellon fellowship in the urban humanities and a publication grant from the Graham Foundation. Explicating the conjunction of planning and occultism in the early twentieth century, the book examines the designation of planned urban space as a site for forming a global ethos—meaning both an outlook on oneself as inescapably linked to every creature and thing, as well as the obligation to choose and act with a regard for one's inexorable impact on others. A similar attention to forms of rhetorical action that sustain notions of belonging informs Shiben's coedited volume In the Shadows of Democracy(link is external) (Intermezzo, 2025). Shiben is currently writing Time on the Road to Civil Rights, which foregrounds the salience of planning in civil rights discourse to advance a genealogical critique of the synchronic emergence of rhetorical theory and planning theory in the mid-twentieth century. He has also begun editing an anthology of uses and meanings of "spirit" in twentieth-century aesthetic, economic, and political thought. A dedicated teacher, Shiben was named Faculty of the Year by his students at the School of Art of Institute of Chicago when he was an Assistant Professor. To encourage new lines of graduate research, Shiben regularly contributes to Oxford Bibliographies in Architecture, Planning, and Preservation. ______ The South Asia Art Initiative (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/saai) at the University of California, Berkeley promotes research-based conversations and collaborations around the arts of South Asia + its diasporas from the ancient period to the now. To read more about the Initiative and help support its various fundraising goals, please click HERE (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/saai) ______ Event made possible with the support of the Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/sarah-kailath-chair-memorial-lecture) Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) Follow us on TWITTER (https://twitter.com/ISASatBerkeley) The event is FREE and OPEN to the public.

events.description: The Institute and Pakistan@Berkeley (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/berkeley-pakistan-initiative), a campaign to broaden and deepen Pakistan related research, teaching and programming at UC Berkeley, are proud to announce the eleventh "Mahomedali Habib Distinguished Lecture on Pakistan (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/mahomedali-habib-lecture-series)" by the award winning writer and novelist, Kamila Shamsie (https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/697055/best-of-friends-by-kamila-shamsie/). Join us as the acclaimed Pakistani writer talks about her craft, and journey, and her latest novel, Best of Friends, with Harsha Ram (https://vcresearch.berkeley.edu/faculty/harsha-ram), Associate Professor in the Departments of Comparative Literature and of Slavic Languages and Literatures, UC Berkeley. Event moderated by Munis D. Faruqui (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/munis-d-faruqui/), Director, Institute for South Asia Studies; Director, Global, International & Area Studies (GIAS); Sarah Kailath Chair of India Studies; Professor, South & Southeast Asian Studies, UC Berkeley. _________________ This event will be live streamed on the Institute's FB page: ISASatUCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) _________________Author Bio Kamila Shamsie is the author of eight novels, which have been translated into over 30 languages, including Burnt Shadows and A God in Every Stone. Her previous novel Home Fire won the Women's Prize for Fiction, was long listed for the Man Booker Prize and shortlisted for the Australian Book Industry Award for International Book. A Vice-President and Fellow of the Royal Society of Literature and Professor of Creative Writing at the University of Manchester, she was one of Granta's 'Best of Young British Novelists' in 2013. She grew up in Karachi, and now lives in London. Her new novel is Best of Friends, published in September 2022. _________________ Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/pages/Center-for-South-Asia-Studies/76502306608) The event is FREE and OPEN to the public.

events.title: The Alan Dundes Lecture featuring Walter Rossa: "From Indo-Portuguese to Goan: the Role of Folk Expressions in Architecture"
events.location: Constance Chiang Pan Anthropology Reading Room
events.description: From Indo-Portuguese to Goan: the Role of Folk Expressions in Architecture In recent decades, scholarship on the Portuguese legacy in artistic expressions in Asia has hesitated to move beyond the global taxonomy of Indo-Portuguese, especially because of the difficulties of choosing or assuming the obvious terms on a case-by-case basis. Nationalisms, in the context of the nation-state crisis and religious-ethnic conflicts, are key clues to explaining this hesitation. Goan Catholic architecture is omnipresent in the promotional material of that fast-developing Indian state, an indisputable emblem of its brand and identity. What has defined its distinctive expression, its architectural grammar and discourse? In this lecture, I will present my contribution: between the colonial and the Goan, folk played a decisive role. Walter Rossa (Caracas, 1962), Architect (Lisbon, 1985), MA in History of Art (Lisbon, 1991), PhD and aggregated in Architecture (Coimbra, 2001 and 2013). Professor in the Department of Architecture and researcher at the Centre for the History of Society and Culture of the University of Coimbra. He holds the UNESCO Chair in Intercultural Dialogue in Heritages of Portuguese Influence (2019) and teaches courses in cultural heritage, town and regional planning, urban design, history, and architecture. Beyond his past work as a practising architect and town planner, he dedicated his efforts last year to cooperation and the relationship among heritage, history, planning, and development. He seeks to establish links between his academic work and development cooperation activities. A significant set of his publications is available at https://coimbra.academia.edu/WalterRossa

events.title: Ayesha S. ​Mahmud | Infectious Diseases in an Era of Global Change: Examples from Bangladesh
events.description: A talk by Ayesha S. ​Mahmud (https://publichealth.berkeley.edu/people/ayesha-mahmud), Associate Professor of Demography, UC Berkeley on the demographic and climatic drivers of infectious diseases in Bangladesh, with broader implications for the future burden of infectious diseases globally.Lawrence Cohen (https://sseas.berkeley.edu/people/lawrence-cohen), Professor of Anthropology and of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Chair, Department of South & Southeast Asian Studies; Co-Director, Medical Anthropology Program, UC Berkeley, will serve as discussant. Event moderated by Elora Shehabuddin (https://gws.berkeley.edu/people/elora-shehabuddin), Professor of Gender & Women's Studies and Global Studies; Faculty Director, Subir and Malini Chowdhury Center for Bangladesh Studies; Faculty Director, Global Studies and Global Poverty and Practice (https://blumcenter.berkeley.edu/academics/gppminor/), UC Berkeley. This event will be live streamed on the Chowdhury Center's FB page: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter). ————–DATE: Tue, April 13, 2027 TIME: 5-6:30 pm PST VENUE: 10 Stephens Hall LIVESTREAM: ChowdhuryCenter@UCBerkeley (https://www.facebook.com/ChowdhuryCenter) —————- ABSTRACT The ecological landscape of our planet is increasingly being shaped by a combination of global demographic shifts, such as rapid urbanization and increased human connectivity, and climatic changes, such as increases in mean temperatures and a greater frequency of extreme weather events. These global changes have important consequences for the emergence, evolution, geographic spread, and burden of infectious diseases. This talk will present insights from recent work on the demographic and climatic drivers of infectious diseases in Bangladesh, with broader implications for the future burden of infectious diseases globally. SPEAKER BIOAyesha S. ​Mahmud (https://publichealth.berkeley.edu/people/ayesha-mahmud) is an Associate Professor of Demography at UC Berkeley. Her research broadly examines the interplay between population change, environmental factors, and infectious disease dynamics. Drawing on theory and methods from demography and disease ecology, her work explores questions such as why outbreaks occur at particular times of year, how and why the mortality burden of infectious diseases changes over time, how population mobility shapes the spatial dynamics of outbreaks, and how global environmental and demographic change may alter patterns of infectious disease burden in the future. She uses statistical methods and biologically mechanistic models to investigate these questions across a range of diseases and settings in Asia, Africa, and Central America, drawing on data from disease surveillance systems, hospital databases, climate models, human mobility data, and population surveys and censuses. Prior to joining UC Berkeley, Mahmud was a Rockefeller Foundation Planetary Health Fellow at Harvard University. She received her PhD in Demography from Princeton University in 2017.Event Poster TBA —————— Event is FREE and OPEN to the public. Like us on FACEBOOK (https://www.facebook.com/ISASatUCBerkeley)PARKING INFORMATION (http://southasia.berkeley.edu/parking-around-campus)Please note that parking in not always easily available in Berkeley. Take public transportation if possible or arrive early to secure your spot.DIRECTIONS (https://southasia.berkeley.edu/contactsdirections) We are located at 10 Stephens Hall on UC Berkeley's campus. Please click this Google Maps Link (https://www.google.com/maps/dir//Institute+for+South+Asia+Studies,+Berkeley,+CA/@37.8712099,-122.3278764,12z/data=!4m9!4m8!1m0!1m5!1m1!1s0x80857c25babcc33d:0xe2ff7d5c1483db5a!2m2!1d-122.2576645!2d37.8710952!3e0) and enter your point of departure.
